phase_title: Sulpician concessions on the chemin du Roy
name_en: Stone house of the French tradition
name_fr: La maison de pierre de tradition française
source_ref: Répertoire du patrimoine culturel du Québec, fiches 93274 (site patrimonial Le Ber-Le Moyne, Lachine), 93440 (maison Rangé-dit-Laviolette, Baie-D'Urfé) et 92796 (maison Hyacinthe-Jamme-dit-Carrière, Pointe-Claire); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissements de Lachine, de Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé et de Pointe-Claire (2005)
source_generation: three RPCQ statements of heritage value (valeur patrimoniale + éléments caractéristiques) read against three sector-characterisation cahiers; no source publishes a per-type table for any West Island place, so the five columns are assembled from the three classed or cited houses themselves
roofing: cedar shingle at Le Ber-Le Moyne; ribbed copper sheet at Pointe-Claire today, over an original wood shingle
siting_landscape: Each of the three survivors sits on ground that predates the street grid around it. Le Ber-Le Moyne stands on a raised point of land beside lac Saint-Louis at the head of the Lachine rapids, on a slight mound planted with mature trees. | The Baie-D'Urfé house stands at the back of its lot, about a hundred metres from the public road and close to the shore, its main front turned south to the lake and the îles Sainte-Geneviève — RPCQ reads that orientation as evidence that the chemin du Roy once ran between the house and the water. | Pointe-Claire's house stands at the far end of a large treed lot that now isolates it from the postwar subdivision around it, on a censive conceded by the Sulpicians in 1722 along the côte Saint-Jean.
massing: A low stone carré on a near-square or short rectangular plan, one and a half storeys, sitting close to the ground. The Baie-D'Urfé carré measures 9.4 by 9.3 m. | Steep two-slope roof with straight slopes. Eaves are shallow at Lachine, and carried out over a covered gallery at Baie-D'Urfé and Pointe-Claire — in both cases a nineteenth-century alteration, not an original feature. | Ancillary buildings belong to the type where they survive - Lachine keeps a stone dépendance of the same date, and an 1781 census records a house, a barn and a stable at Baie-D'Urfé.
articulation: Almost none in the original fabric. What ornament these houses carry — moulded wood chambranles, gable dormers, a neo-Gothic porch, a bell-cast eave — was added between about 1828 and 1874 to bring them up to date.
openings: Openings set out asymmetrically, which RPCQ names as a French-tradition trait at both Baie-D'Urfé and Pointe-Claire. | Casement windows with small panes. At Pointe-Claire the south front is opened up for light while the north wall carries only two windows.
materials: Fieldstone throughout, laid up rubble. Pointe-Claire is left bare, and RPCQ names the absence of crépi as a Montréal-region trait; Baie-D'Urfé is whitewashed on three sides. | Two chimney stacks carried up in the line of the gable walls — the trait RPCQ singles out as belonging "plus particulièrement" to the houses of the island of Montréal and its neighbouring regions.
conservation: All three houses are protected individually, and none of the three village or shore ensembles around them is. Lachine's is a classed site patrimonial (2001) covering the exteriors and the land; Pointe-Claire's is a classed immeuble patrimonial (1964-08-12) covering exterior, interior and land; Baie-D'Urfé's is a municipal citation (2001) covering only the exterior envelope of the oldest, eastern section.
blurb_en: A low fieldstone box of one and a half storeys under a steep two-slope roof, stacks rising inside the gable walls, openings placed where they were wanted rather than where symmetry asked for them. Three of them survive across three of the six West Island places — a trading post of 1669–71 at Lachine, a farm house of about 1700 at Baie-D'Urfé, and one of 1769–91 at Pointe-Claire — and all three are protected individually while nothing around them is. One record, three municipalities: the photograph on this card is Lachine's, and Baie-D'Urfé's and Pointe-Claire's stand beside it on the type page.
origin_en: The Sulpicians became seigneurs of the island of Montréal in 1663 and conceded the côtes that run out to its western end; the houses built on those concessions were stone because stone was what the fields gave up and because fire and raiding made anything else a poor bet. What survives is very little. Lachine's is the oldest and least altered: two rectangular stone buildings put up in 1669–71 as a fur-trade post for Charles Le Moyne and Jacques Le Ber, restored in the 1980s toward their seventeenth-century appearance and now the Musée de Lachine. Baie-D'Urfé's was built about 1700 by Hubert Rangé dit Laviolette on a concession he bought in 1695, and then quietly rebuilt by the Pilon family between 1839 and 1874 — the walls raised, the roof pitch eased off, moulded chambranles and projecting eaves added in what RPCQ calls a taste imported after the Conquest. Pointe-Claire's went up between 1769 and 1791 on a censive conceded in 1722, and was altered again in 1828. Read together the three make the point the West Island pages keep making: the form is one form across three municipalities, the protection is three separate individual instruments granted in 1964, 2001 and 2001, and not one of them protects an ensemble.

phase_title: The population quintuples, and the merger
source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), § 1.2.2 « Les ensembles urbains d'intérêt » et secteurs 7.U.1 à 7.U.8 (Dorval), 5.U.2 et 5.U.3 (Pointe-Claire), 19.U.2 (Lachine), 2.U.2 et 2.U.4 (Pierrefonds-Senneville) et 2.E.4 (Senneville), avec le § 2 Historique de l'arrondissement de Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé
source_generation: five sector-characterisation cahiers of the same 2005 series, read together; the series created a category, Ensembles urbains d'intérêt, expressly to catch postwar suburban housing, and that category is the only per-type writing any West Island source does
siting_landscape: Detached on its own lot, set back from the street with side margins, and with parking in the front yard — the Lachine cahier's description of the same wave, and the one place any West Island source describes the siting rule rather than the building. | Cul-de-sac and crescent street patterns recur, sometimes with a planted median down a wide avenue, and Dorval's cahier ties the effect of every one of these sectors to mature trees on the properties rather than to the houses. | Built in small series from a short catalogue of models. Dorval's 7.U.5 is praised for using « un nombre relativement restreint de modèles » while letting the materials vary house to house; Lachine's 19.U.2 calls the catalogue of types on its territory « particulièrement impressionnant ». In Lachine the dominant form of that catalogue is not this one but the taller contractor's box known locally as the maison « Gameroff », which carries its own record on that page; what belongs here is the alignment of Californian-inspired bungalows the cahier singles out at the end of the 51e Avenue.
massing: One storey, plain-pied. The Dorval cahier repeats the phrase « bungalows de type plain-pied, toit pavillon, brique » for two separate sectors, 7.U.1 and 7.U.4, and treats it as the norm for the municipality from the 1940s–50s onward. | A hipped roof is the commonest form. Lachine records more variety in the same years — pitched, hipped, or hipped combined with a false mansard. | Split-level versions appear in the same wave and the same decade; Dorval's 7.U.5 dates a whole quadrilateral of them to the 1950s.
articulation: Almost none, and what there is varies within a single street rather than between streets. Dorval's Model Homes are described as houses that look alike until you look closely, at which point the window types, the roofs, the use of artificial stone and clapboard and the handling of the brick are all different.
openings: Not described by any West Island source beyond the note that window types differ between otherwise identical Dorval houses.
materials: Brick dominant, with artificial stone and clapboard used as accent — the three materials Dorval's cahier names on avenue Dahlia. | Red brick at Pointe-Claire's Magil project, built 1953–55.
conservation: This is the only wave in the West Island whose recognition is explicitly experimental. The 2005 series says its own identification of these sectors « est exploratoire » and aims to link them to conservation concerns « pour une première fois ». | Where the cahiers return to it, they say the same thing twice - the value lies in the plan, the planting and the consistency of the materials rather than in any individual house, and personalisation is what erodes it. Lachine's 19.U.2 records that practically every building in its sector has been modified, and lists how: raising, building to the lot line, added upper storeys or a garage, changed cladding, changed openings, changed roof form. | Pointe-Claire's veterans' sector is the sharpest case: the cahier says few of the wartime houses are left and that what still marks the sector is the street layout and the subdivision, not the buildings.
blurb_en: One storey, hipped roof, brick with artificial stone and clapboard for variety, a carport or a garage, a cul-de-sac and mature trees. Built from a short catalogue of models across all six West Island places from the late 1940s, and the only twentieth-century housing the 2005 evaluation series took seriously enough to invent a category for.
origin_en: The wave arrives at different moments and for different reasons. At Dorval it is the airport: the aerodrome opened in 1941, air traffic grew fast after the war, the rest of the territory was opened to subdivision and the population went from under 3,000 in the 1940s to more than 20,000 by 1971. At Pointe-Claire it is a straight housing shortage — a veterans' sector on the Wartime Housing Limited model about 1947, then the Magil project of 1953–55. At Lachine it is what the cahier calls « l'urbanisation massive des années 1950-1970 », running east across the last open ground and producing a catalogue of contractors' types so consistent that the dominant one is still known locally by its builder's name. At Baie-D'Urfé it is the Métropolitaine and the demographic boom together, pushing settlement north across the railway for the first time. What the 2005 cahiers do with all of it is the interesting part. The series invented a category, Ensembles urbains d'intérêt, to hold postwar suburbs, said openly that the exercise was exploratory, and then valued these places for their street layouts, their planting and the consistency of their materials rather than for their architecture — while recording, in the same paragraphs, that almost every house had already been raised, extended, re-clad or re-roofed. It is the one wave on these six pages that the source treats as heritage-in-progress rather than as heritage.
photo_credit: The only photographs of West Island postwar bungalows located during this research are the 2005 Ville de Montréal évaluation cahiers' own — Dorval, p. 30–31, captioned « 7.U.1 165, rue McNicoll », « 7.U.2 1, avenue Dalhia », « 7.U.3 70, avenue des Lilas », « 7.U.4 Vue d'ensemble » and « 7.U.6 Avenue Claude »; Pointe-Claire, p. 34, « 5.U.2 Le 105 de l'avenue de Windward Crescent »; Lachine, p. 40, « 19.U.2 La 53e Avenue » and « 19.U.2 Une maison "Gameroff" typique au 3, 40e avenue ». © Ville de Montréal; not reproduced here. Wikimedia Commons was searched for a freely licensed photograph of a postwar bungalow in any of the six places and none was found. The one candidate that looked promising by its address — « Quatre-Vents, 12, avenue Dahlia (Dorval) », on the Model Homes street itself — was downloaded and inspected and is not a bungalow at all but a two-and-a-half-storey stuccoed house with a tiled coping and an arcaded loggia, so it was rejected. The Cité de Dorval's own heritage study of that address (LEMAYMICHAUD + Réal Paul architecte, « Expertise historique et étude patrimoniale, 12, avenue Dahlia, Dorval ») confirms the rejection and dates the house to 1803, enlarged 1874–85 in a neo-Gothic manner and wholly remade 1927–37 into the Italianate it wears now — one of the first stone houses in the district, standing on the street the bungalows were later built along, and not one of them. The same study independently repeats the cahier's figures for the 1951 project - 28 dwellings, 12 detached and 16 semi-detached bungalows, and two apartment buildings.

phase_title: The radial bourg and the French-inspired farmhouse
source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), p. 48
source_generation: Plan de conservation narrative typology, the paragraph plus the bulleted list headed « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type », transcribed verbatim
siting_landscape: Generally set without regard to the public road, its principal façade turned south for the most sunlight — the sharpest siting rule in this part, and the opposite of Île d'Orléans, where the chemin Royal governs. | The oldest dwelling type in the site. Survivors stand mainly on the ceinture, the old farm lots outside the Trait-Carré.
massing: Almost square or rectangular plan, of modest dimensions, one and a half storeys. | Barely raised off the ground, with squat proportions. | Two straight steeply pitched slopes, covered in wood shingle.
articulation: The plan lists no ornament for this type at all — the whole description is plan, roof, walls, openings and chimneys.
openings: Asymmetrically disposed; wood casement windows with small panes.
materials: Walls of pièce-sur-pièce or of stone, the stone usually rendered and whitewashed. | One or two chimney stacks emerging from the roof.
blurb_en: The oldest house in the site and the only one that ignores the road: a low, squat, one-and-a-half storey box of pièce-sur-pièce or whitewashed rendered stone, under two straight steep slopes of wood shingle, with one or two stacks and small-paned casements set wherever the inside wanted them. Its façade faces south for the sun, whatever direction the Trait-Carré happens to run.
origin_en: The house of the Régime français, built on the trapezoidal farm lots the Jesuits conceded from 1665 and, under the règle du tiers, always in the first third of the lot against the Trait-Carré. The plan de conservation warns that this type is easier to see than to date: several 18th-century houses were altered so heavily that their apparent age is nothing like their real one — 8180-8182 Le Trait-Carré Est was built about 1724 and given a mansard roof in 1931 — while the maison Éphraïm-Bédard looks like a French-inspired farmhouse and was built about a century later.

phase_title: The neoclassical village and Baillairgé's church
source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), p. 49
source_generation: Plan de conservation narrative typology, the paragraph plus the bulleted list headed « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type », transcribed verbatim
roofing: bardeaux de cèdre ou tôle traditionnelle à la canadienne ou à baguettes
siting_landscape: The type that marks the whole 19th century in the site, and the one that fills the Trait-Carré on both sides.
massing: Rectangular plan, raised off the ground to give a rudimentary cellar. | Two-slope roof with overhanging larmiers, sometimes upturned. | A summer kitchen sometimes repeats the volume of the house at reduced scale, set back against the north-east wall or perpendicular at the rear.
articulation: A gallery running along the façade, sheltered by the overhanging larmier — a transitional space between inside and out, often decorated with ornamental woodwork. | Openings framed by moulded wood chambranles.
openings: Many wood casement windows with large panes, rectangular and vertically proportioned, usually set symmetrically about the door at the centre of the façade.
materials: Pièce-sur-pièce or madrier-sur-madrier structure. | Vertical or horizontal plank cladding, or fieldstone rendered and whitewashed. In wood or in masonry alike, these houses are white.
blurb_en: The 19th-century village house, and the one the Trait-Carré is mostly made of: a rectangular white box raised just enough for a rough cellar, with the roof's larmiers reaching out past the wall — often curving up as they go — to shelter a gallery running the whole width of the façade. Large-paned casements sit symmetrically either side of a central door in moulded frames, and a summer kitchen often repeats the house in miniature at the back.
origin_en: The plan makes it an explicitly post-Conquest form: British know-how, changing construction technique and changing ways of living produce a new type that "marque tout le XIXe siècle", while keeping the rectangular plan and the sloped roof of the French model. It is the same house Saint-Lambert, Terrebonne, Lévis, Québec City and Île d'Orléans each catalogue under their own names, and the Charlesbourg description is the one that insists on the colour.

phase_title: Mansards and the institutional build-out
source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), pp. 49–50
source_generation: Plan de conservation narrative typology, the paragraph plus the bulleted list headed « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type », transcribed verbatim
roofing: as the neoclassical type — cedar shingle or traditional tin
siting_landscape: Appears in the last quarter of the 19th century, and the plan's statistics show how far it spread — 27 of the site's 138 principal buildings, about 19 %, carry a mansard roof. | Its earliest examples here favour the four-slope mansard, as on the former couvent des Soeurs du Bon-Pasteur; the two-slope version is used more from the turn of the 20th century.
massing: Rectangular plan, tending to lengthen relative to the individual houses of the preceding types. | A mansard roof of gently pitched terrasson over a nearly vertical brisis, generally of two slopes, with four-slope and hipped variants.
articulation: Sometimes elaborate ornament — decorative woodwork on galleries, on dormers and around the openings.
openings: Symmetrically disposed, sometimes arched, of vertical proportion; often wood casements with large panes.
materials: Made of the same materials as the Québec house of neoclassical inspiration.
blurb_en: A rectangular plan that stretches longer than the houses before it, under a roof of gentle terrasson over an almost vertical brisis — two slopes usually, four or hipped sometimes. Symmetrical, vertically proportioned openings, occasionally arched, and ornament that can turn elaborate: decorative woodwork on the galleries, on the dormers and round the windows. Its materials are simply those of the neoclassical house it succeeds.
origin_en: The plan traces the route explicitly: monumental Paris under Napoleon III, reintroducing a roof form of the French classical period; then Québec's institutional buildings and bourgeois houses; then convents and presbyteries; then, quickly, rural domestic architecture. Charlesbourg shows the whole chain in one place — the presbytery of 1875, the convent of 1883 and the sacristy of 1887 are all Second Empire, and the houses follow. The plan is also candid that some mansards here are retro-fits: a few old houses got one to make the attic habitable.

phase_title: Vernaculaire industriel
source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), p. 51
source_generation: Plan de conservation, the sub-variant bullet inside « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type » for the maison vernaculaire industrielle, transcribed verbatim
style_label: Boomtown (false front) / Vernaculaire industriel (Québec industrial vernacular)
siting_landscape: Flat roofs account for 31 of the site's 138 principal buildings, about 22 %, and the plan says most of them date from the 20th century. | The oldest flat roof in the site is not a house at all but a former forge at 7821 Le Trait-Carré Est, built between 1863 and 1886.
massing: Distinguished by its flat or low-pitched roof, concealed behind a parapet.
articulation: Inherited from the parent type — standardised architectural elements, doors and windows. The parapet is the type's defining articulation.

materials: Machined materials; the parent type's beams, boards and asbestos-cement tile.
blurb_en: One line in the plan and nothing more: a flat or barely sloping roof hidden behind a parapet. It is the shopkeeper's end of the industrial vernacular, and at Charlesbourg it belongs with the fourteen buildings that put a shop on the ground floor and a dwelling above it.
origin_en: Boomtown is now the most widely distributed form on this site, catalogued at Saint-Lambert, Gatineau, Québec City, Trois-Rivières, Lévis, Île d'Orléans and here. Charlesbourg is the case where it is filed as a sub-variant rather than a type, and where the plan shows the parapet jumping category: the salle paroissiale of 1925, now the salle Pierre-Garon, borrows it for a parish hall.

phase_title: Vernaculaire industriel
source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), p. 51
source_generation: Plan de conservation, the sub-variant bullet inside « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type » for the maison vernaculaire industrielle, transcribed verbatim
style_label: American Foursquare / Vernaculaire industriel (Québec industrial vernacular)
siting_landscape: The plan notes that most of the site's pavilion roofs sit on two-storey cubic houses built in the first decades of the 20th century.
massing: Distinguished by a square plan of two storeys. | Low-pitched pavilion roof, sometimes with a dormer on the front slope.
articulation: Inherited from the parent type — standardised architectural elements, doors and windows.
openings: Rectangular openings of vertical proportion; wood windows, casement or sash.

blurb_en: A square plan two storeys high under a shallow pavilion roof, sometimes with a single dormer on the front slope, clad in horizontal boards or brick. The plan gives it three lines and no more — which is itself the point: the whole appeal of the industrial vernacular was that it needed no more than three lines to describe.
origin_en: The same American Foursquare that Saint-Lambert, Gatineau, Québec City, Trois-Rivières, Lévis and Île d'Orléans all catalogue. What differs at Charlesbourg is its rank: here it is a sub-variant inside the maison vernaculaire industrielle rather than a courant of its own, and the plan's built-fabric survey confirms it arrived with the century, putting most of the site's pavilion roofs on two-storey cubic houses of the first decades of the 20th century.

phase_title: Vernaculaire industriel
source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), pp. 50–51
source_generation: Plan de conservation narrative typology, the paragraph plus the bulleted list headed « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type », transcribed verbatim. The last three bullets each define one sub-variant and are carried on the three child records.
siting_landscape: From the end of the 19th century until the Second World War, this is the type that dominates new building in the site — the plan's words are "le type qui domine les nouvelles constructions".
massing: A simplified volume. A light frame, also called "Balloon Frame". | Suits the single-family dwelling but can also hold two.
articulation: Standardised architectural elements, such as doors and windows.
openings: Rectangular openings of vertical proportion; wood windows, casement or sash.
materials: Machined materials — beams and boards. New materials appearing at the start of the 20th century, such as asbestos-cement tile.
blurb_en: The type that took over. From the 1890s to the Second World War it is what got built here: a simplified volume on a balloon frame, machined beams and boards, catalogue doors and windows, asbestos-cement tile, rectangular vertically proportioned casements or sashes — cheap, simple and adaptable enough to hold one household or two. The plan then splits it three ways: cubique, cottage vernaculaire, Boomtown.
origin_en: Standardised materials, mechanised labour and plans distributed at continental scale through catalogues and magazines produced this architecture in the United States; it came to Canada and spread on the strength of how simple and cheap it was to build. Charlesbourg's plan de conservation is one of the two Québec sources on this site that treat the three forms as one family with a parent — the Ville de Québec thésaurus is the other — while the MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans and the Ville de Lévis list them as separate courants of equal rank. Nothing in the buildings changes; the disagreement is entirely about the level of the category.
photo_credit: Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), fig. 31 — the plan's own three-photograph strip showing, in order, 723-725-727 boulevard Louis-XIV, 8210 Le Trait-Carré Est and 7868 Le Trait-Carré Est. © Gouvernement du Québec, ministère de la Culture et des Communications. Not reproduced.

phase_title: Vernaculaire industriel
source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), p. 51
source_generation: Plan de conservation, the sub-variant bullet inside « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type » for the maison vernaculaire industrielle, transcribed verbatim
siting_landscape: Reads at a glance as the traditional Québec house it stands beside on the Trait-Carré; the difference is in the eave.
massing: Compares to the Québec house of neoclassical inspiration in its general form. | But its eave differs — the larmier has no coyaux, and its pitch is slightly shallower. | A variant sets the façade on the gable wall.
articulation: Inherited from the parent type — standardised architectural elements, doors and windows.
openings: Rectangular openings of vertical proportion; wood windows, casement or sash.
materials: Machined materials; the parent type's beams, boards and asbestos-cement tile.
blurb_en: The industrial vernacular wearing the traditional house's clothes. In general form it is the Québec house of neoclassical inspiration; what gives it away is the eave, where the larmier runs out straight because there is no coyau under it, on a pitch that is slightly shallower. One variant turns the façade onto the gable wall.
origin_en: The plan's sentence on this form is the most useful in the whole part, because it is the only place in these sources where a document says plainly what separates a mass-produced house from the handbuilt one it copies — and the answer is a single missing piece of carpentry. The coyau is fiddly work; the balloon frame and the catalogue plan dispensed with it. This is the same form the Île d'Orléans inventory calls the cottage vernaculaire américain, Lévis calls the vernaculaire américain, and Québec City catalogues as the cottage vernaculaire industriel.

phase_title: Suburbanisation, cité, merger
source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), p. 51
source_generation: Plan de conservation narrative typology, the paragraph plus the bulleted list headed « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type », transcribed verbatim
siting_landscape: Arrives at the turn of the 1950s, when sprawl subdivides the farm lots and bungalows go up across the site. | The plan counts 26 buildings of one storey, "majoritairement des bungalows érigés après la Deuxième Guerre mondiale", and 15 buildings clad in the non-traditional brick-and-artificial-stone combination, "principalement des bungalows".
massing: Rectangular or rather square plan. | Generally one storey. | Low-profile pavilion roof, or hipped.
articulation: The plan names no ornament for this type.
openings: The plan gives no opening description for this type.
materials: Mixed cladding of brick and artificial stone.
blurb_en: A rectangular or nearly square plan, one storey, a low pavilion or hipped roof, and brick mixed with artificial stone. Four lines is all the plan gives it — and yet more than a third of everything standing inside this declared site went up between 1925 and 1975.
origin_en: The bungalow is what the declaration of 1965 was reacting to. Sprawl reached Charlesbourg at the turn of the 1950s and cut up the farm lots; the plan records that 65 buildings, 48.5 % of the site, date from 1925–1975, and that most of the site's 26 single-storey buildings are post-war bungalows. The 2005 Étude de caractérisation makes the same point from the other side: by 1963 urban sprawl had already reached the ceinture, much of the agricultural heritage had gone, and the perimeter drawn in 1965 enclosed "le produit (la zone d'occupation villageoise) plutôt que la source (ce qu'il restait des terres agricoles à l'origine du village)".

phase_title: The railway, the villégiature and the village
name_en: English summer villa on the lake shore
source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissement de Dorval–L'Île-Dorval (2005), § 2 et secteurs 7.E.3 à 7.E.6, 7.I.1 à 7.I.5, et arrondissement de Pierrefonds-Senneville (2005), secteur 2.E.4 Grandes propriétés de Senneville; Parcs Canada, Répertoire des désignations patrimoniales fédérales, arrondissement historique de Senneville, id 1973
source_generation: two sector-characterisation cahiers read with one federal designation record; no source publishes a per-type table for either place
siting_landscape: Free-standing on a large treed lot between the shore road and the water, set well back from the road and, at Senneville, deliberately screened from it — Parks Canada records that the siting and planting of most Senneville houses "prevents a view to the buildings from chemin Senneville". | At Dorval the belt runs along the chemin du Bord-du-Lac, the old shore road, and out onto the points that reach into lac Saint-Louis. Île Dorval was divided into 57 lots for summer houses in 1911 and is still reachable only by ferry. | Boat clubs, a yacht club, horse racing and golf belong to the same siting. The Dorval cahier treats them as part of the phase, not as background.
massing: Two to two and a half storeys, informal in plan, with the volumes and roofs put together loosely rather than symmetrically — the Senneville fiche says the houses « agencent des volumes nets et des toitures importantes de façon plus ou moins complexe ». | Large roofs carrying dormers, and deep verandahs across the front, often arcaded on heavy rubble piers. | Smaller and plainer versions of the same idea line the same shore — the modest one-storey chalets and cottages of Dorval's avenue Saint-Charles, avenues Roy and Lepage, boulevard Pine Beach and secteur Ouest, many later converted to year-round houses.
articulation: Wide arched openings under the verandah roof, heavy stone piers, shingled wall planes carried unbroken around corners.
openings: Grouped windows, often in twos and threes, in plain flat casings; no source gives a proportion.
materials: Wood shingle over the upper walls and the roof; rubble or cut stone below. The Senneville fiche lists « revêtements de pierre taillée ou de moellons, brique, bois, stuc et toitures en bardeaux de cèdre ». | Fieldstone alone where the building is earlier or plainer — Dorval's chapelle St. Mark of 1898, built « en pierre des champs » for the Protestant summer people, and the stone manor Alfred Brown called Bel-Air.
conservation: Senneville's villas fall inside a National Historic Site, which is a federal commemorative designation and not a control on private alteration. Dorval's have no ensemble instrument of any kind. | Both cahiers name attrition as the live risk. Dorval's says speculation on shore land and the disappearance of the great properties or of their lot patterns is a problem to be reckoned with, and that speculation on old houses and their lots for large new houses works against the village character. The Senneville fiche records « un morcellement des lots des grandes propriétés et à la densification rapide du territoire ». | Two of the named Dorval villas are already gone — Ashburton, built about 1879, and the McConnell stone manor that replaced it, burned in 1963.
blurb_en: The summer house of anglophone Montréal on the western lake shore — free-standing in its own grounds, set back and screened from the road, two to two and a half storeys of shingle over rubble stone, big loose roofs and a deep arcaded verandah facing the water. The railway of 1855 made it possible; sailing, golf and horse racing came with it; and at Dorval speculation on the shore has already taken the two largest of them. One record, two municipalities: the photograph on this card is Senneville's Wanklyn house, and Dorval's maison Beaurivage stands beside it on the type page.
origin_en: From the late nineteenth century the shores of lac Saint-Louis and the lac des Deux-Montagnes became the summer address of bourgeois Montréal, and the train is what did it. At Dorval the village fed both the summer people and the farmers at once, and the resort came with a whole apparatus — sailing, horse racing, golf, a yacht club, a Protestant chapel of fieldstone built for the villégiateurs in 1898. Île Dorval, bought in 1853 by Sir George Simpson of the Hudson's Bay Company for a summer house in the woods, was cut into fifty-seven lots in 1911, and about fifteen families were summering there by the 1930s; it is still only reachable by boat. At Senneville the same impulse produced something denser and grander, a dozen estates along one country road with their houses turned to the lake and hidden from the chemin, and Parks Canada designated the whole of it. The two places show the same form at two scales, and they show the same erosion: the Senneville fiche records the great lots being cut up and the territory densifying, and Dorval's records speculation on shore land, the disappearance of the great properties and new houses of a size that breaks the street. Ashburton of about 1879 is gone. The stone manor that J. W. McConnell built after it burned in 1963. What is left of that property is the entrance pavilion and one summer house in its gardens.
photo_credit: « Maison Beaurivage, 900, chemin du Bord-du-Lac (Dorval) », photo Anne-Marie Dufour, 2010-11-19, Flickr stream *Parcours riverain — Ville de Montréal*; Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0, Flickr licence review passed (verified through the Commons API).

phase_title: The airport and the bungalow suburb
source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), § 1.2.2 « Les ensembles urbains d'intérêt » et secteurs 7.U.1 à 7.U.8 (Dorval), 5.U.2 et 5.U.3 (Pointe-Claire), 19.U.2 (Lachine), 2.U.2 et 2.U.4 (Pierrefonds-Senneville) et 2.E.4 (Senneville), avec le § 2 Historique de l'arrondissement de Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé
source_generation: five sector-characterisation cahiers of the same 2005 series, read together; the series created a category, Ensembles urbains d'intérêt, expressly to catch postwar suburban housing, and that category is the only per-type writing any West Island source does
siting_landscape: Detached on its own lot, set back from the street with side margins, and with parking in the front yard — the Lachine cahier's description of the same wave, and the one place any West Island source describes the siting rule rather than the building. | Cul-de-sac and crescent street patterns recur, sometimes with a planted median down a wide avenue, and Dorval's cahier ties the effect of every one of these sectors to mature trees on the properties rather than to the houses. | Built in small series from a short catalogue of models. Dorval's 7.U.5 is praised for using « un nombre relativement restreint de modèles » while letting the materials vary house to house; Lachine's 19.U.2 calls the catalogue of types on its territory « particulièrement impressionnant ». In Lachine the dominant form of that catalogue is not this one but the taller contractor's box known locally as the maison « Gameroff », which carries its own record on that page; what belongs here is the alignment of Californian-inspired bungalows the cahier singles out at the end of the 51e Avenue.
massing: One storey, plain-pied. The Dorval cahier repeats the phrase « bungalows de type plain-pied, toit pavillon, brique » for two separate sectors, 7.U.1 and 7.U.4, and treats it as the norm for the municipality from the 1940s–50s onward. | A hipped roof is the commonest form. Lachine records more variety in the same years — pitched, hipped, or hipped combined with a false mansard. | Split-level versions appear in the same wave and the same decade; Dorval's 7.U.5 dates a whole quadrilateral of them to the 1950s.
articulation: Almost none, and what there is varies within a single street rather than between streets. Dorval's Model Homes are described as houses that look alike until you look closely, at which point the window types, the roofs, the use of artificial stone and clapboard and the handling of the brick are all different.
openings: Not described by any West Island source beyond the note that window types differ between otherwise identical Dorval houses.
materials: Brick dominant, with artificial stone and clapboard used as accent — the three materials Dorval's cahier names on avenue Dahlia. | Red brick at Pointe-Claire's Magil project, built 1953–55.
conservation: This is the only wave in the West Island whose recognition is explicitly experimental. The 2005 series says its own identification of these sectors « est exploratoire » and aims to link them to conservation concerns « pour une première fois ». | Where the cahiers return to it, they say the same thing twice - the value lies in the plan, the planting and the consistency of the materials rather than in any individual house, and personalisation is what erodes it. Lachine's 19.U.2 records that practically every building in its sector has been modified, and lists how: raising, building to the lot line, added upper storeys or a garage, changed cladding, changed openings, changed roof form. | Pointe-Claire's veterans' sector is the sharpest case: the cahier says few of the wartime houses are left and that what still marks the sector is the street layout and the subdivision, not the buildings.
blurb_en: One storey, hipped roof, brick with artificial stone and clapboard for variety, a carport or a garage, a cul-de-sac and mature trees. Built from a short catalogue of models across all six West Island places from the late 1940s, and the only twentieth-century housing the 2005 evaluation series took seriously enough to invent a category for.
origin_en: The wave arrives at different moments and for different reasons. At Dorval it is the airport: the aerodrome opened in 1941, air traffic grew fast after the war, the rest of the territory was opened to subdivision and the population went from under 3,000 in the 1940s to more than 20,000 by 1971. At Pointe-Claire it is a straight housing shortage — a veterans' sector on the Wartime Housing Limited model about 1947, then the Magil project of 1953–55. At Lachine it is what the cahier calls « l'urbanisation massive des années 1950-1970 », running east across the last open ground and producing a catalogue of contractors' types so consistent that the dominant one is still known locally by its builder's name. At Baie-D'Urfé it is the Métropolitaine and the demographic boom together, pushing settlement north across the railway for the first time. What the 2005 cahiers do with all of it is the interesting part. The series invented a category, Ensembles urbains d'intérêt, to hold postwar suburbs, said openly that the exercise was exploratory, and then valued these places for their street layouts, their planting and the consistency of their materials rather than for their architecture — while recording, in the same paragraphs, that almost every house had already been raised, extended, re-clad or re-roofed. It is the one wave on these six pages that the source treats as heritage-in-progress rather than as heritage.
photo_credit: The only photographs of West Island postwar bungalows located during this research are the 2005 Ville de Montréal évaluation cahiers' own — Dorval, p. 30–31, captioned « 7.U.1 165, rue McNicoll », « 7.U.2 1, avenue Dalhia », « 7.U.3 70, avenue des Lilas », « 7.U.4 Vue d'ensemble » and « 7.U.6 Avenue Claude »; Pointe-Claire, p. 34, « 5.U.2 Le 105 de l'avenue de Windward Crescent »; Lachine, p. 40, « 19.U.2 La 53e Avenue » and « 19.U.2 Une maison "Gameroff" typique au 3, 40e avenue ». © Ville de Montréal; not reproduced here. Wikimedia Commons was searched for a freely licensed photograph of a postwar bungalow in any of the six places and none was found. The one candidate that looked promising by its address — « Quatre-Vents, 12, avenue Dahlia (Dorval) », on the Model Homes street itself — was downloaded and inspected and is not a bungalow at all but a two-and-a-half-storey stuccoed house with a tiled coping and an arcaded loggia, so it was rejected. The Cité de Dorval's own heritage study of that address (LEMAYMICHAUD + Réal Paul architecte, « Expertise historique et étude patrimoniale, 12, avenue Dahlia, Dorval ») confirms the rejection and dates the house to 1803, enlarged 1874–85 in a neo-Gothic manner and wholly remade 1927–37 into the Italianate it wears now — one of the first stone houses in the district, standing on the street the bungalows were later built along, and not one of them. The same study independently repeats the cahier's figures for the 1951 project - 28 dwellings, 12 detached and 16 semi-detached bungalows, and two apartment buildings.

phase_title: After the fires — rebuilding Hull and Aylmer
name_en: Mixed-use building with a flat roof (édifice mixte à toit plat)
source_ref: Ville de Gatineau, fiche « L'édifice mixte à toit plat » (Enclume, 2023)
source_generation: 2023 type fiches (Ville de Gatineau)
siting_landscape: Marked presence in the Aylmer, Hull and Buckingham sectors and, to a lesser extent, in the Gatineau sector.
massing: Flat roof, or of shallow pitch sloping down towards the rear. | Two to three storeys above ground. | Rectangular plan (frequent) or L-shaped plan (occasional). | Trapezoidal plan (following the urban fabric) (occasional). | Corbelled balcony at the upper floor (occasional).
articulation: Cornice crowning the front façade (frequent) and the side façade where the latter borders a street (occasional). | Parapet on the front façade (rare). | Lintels and sills of dressed stone or moulded concrete (frequent), arched brick lintels (occasional) or soldier-course brick (occasional) above the openings. | Entablature surmounting a display window on the façade (frequent). | Pilasters on the façade (occasional). | Datestone on the façade (rare).
openings: Single or double door with a window, surmounted by a transom, at the centre of the façade (frequent), sometimes recessed, or in a corner of the building (occasional), for the entrance to the ground floor. | Single door with or without transom, set off-centre, for access to the upper floors. | Sash windows with or without muntins (frequent). | Windows of vertical format. | Display windows at the ground floor, with (occasional) or without a transom.
materials: Exterior cladding of red or brown brick of Modular format (8" × 2 ½" × 3 ½"), laid in stretcher bond (frequent). | Cladding of wood clapboard or rabbeted (shiplap) boards, sometimes partial (occasional).
conservation: Prefer: Extensions should be built at the rear of the building and remain little visible from the street. In the case of a contemporary rear extension, the new volume could take its cue from the scale and forms of the original extensions or secondary volumes. | Prefer: Preserve the symmetry of the volume and of the façade composition. | Avoid: Avoid removing a projection, significantly changing the shape of its openings, or covering it with materials that do not correspond to the initial materials. | Avoid: Avoid an addition on the front façade that would harm the perception of the original volume. | Prefer: Maintain the original size, arrangement and type of opening as far as possible. | Prefer: Favour a model with a number of muntins/panes similar to the original or to other buildings of the same model built in the same period. | Prefer: The placement of signs should not conceal components of interest. | Avoid: Avoid replacing original openings with openings whose type does not correspond to those identified above. | Prefer: Favour a cladding material in keeping with the original materials identified, such as brick in shades of red or brown. Other complementary materials could however be considered for the addition of a new volume. | Avoid: Avoid choosing a cladding whose appearance or finish does not correspond to the pre-identified original cladding materials for the main body. | Prefer: Original ornamentation should be maintained and kept up, or else replaced as faithfully as possible where its preservation is not possible. | Avoid: Avoid adding ornaments that do not correspond to the pre-identified originals or that never existed on the building. | Avoid: Avoid removing original ornaments without replacing them.
blurb_en: A shop below and dwellings above, in two to three storeys under a roof that is flat or falls gently to the rear. One or two display windows flank the store entrance, taller rectangular windows light the flats, and a cornice or entablature marks where the commercial floor ends and the residential ones begin.
origin_en: The flat-roofed mixed-use building shares many similarities with the brick house with a flat roof. It appears towards the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th, as the commercial arteries of the Hull, Aylmer, Buckingham and Gatineau sectors were developing. In that period, which precedes the modern principle of segregating uses and the arrival of department stores, commercial and residential sectors merged and buildings combined commercial premises on the ground floor with dwellings on the upper floors. Like the brick house with a flat roof, the type is tied to technological change in construction methods and above all to the industrialisation of materials: balloon-frame structures at the end of the 19th century allowed faster construction with standardised materials, and the waterproof roofing membranes that appeared in the 1910s and 1920s permitted shallower roof pitches for drainage.
photo_credit: Enclume. 2023. 495, avenue de Buckingham — Ville de Gatineau. Not reproduced: the City's conditions of use prohibit republication to third parties.

phase_title: Federal-employee suburbanisation

blurb_en: One to one and a half storeys under a straight two-slope roof of low to medium pitch, its ridge generally parallel to the street and its slope frequently carried forward over a front veranda on square wood posts. origin_en: The first-generation North American bungalow takes its name, and was originally influenced by, the spatial arrangement of dwellings in the Bengal region of India, which have a single storey surrounded by a veranda. British colonisers exported the model to the United Kingdom, where the appearance of the bungalow formed part of the Arts & Crafts movement, a social movement promoting a return to craftsmanship in architecture and a pastoral way of life in opposition to the runaway industrialisation of the late 19th century; in North America the movement was reduced largely to its aesthetic dimension. The bungalow was adapted in California around 1905, notably by the architects Charles Sumner Greene and Henry Mather Greene, borrowing certain elements from the Arts & Crafts style, and in the following years it appeared in numerous architectural catalogues that circulated plans for different house models. Economical to build, the first generation of bungalows became extremely popular in the United States, spreading widely through the new suburbs until the 1930s; in Quebec its popularity came somewhat later, running from the 1910s to the 1940s, and it differs significantly from the second generation of bungalows that became popular in the post-war suburbs from the 1950s onward.

Two single glazed doors sit side by side at the centre of the front, frequently behind a shed-roofed veranda on square wood posts.
origin_en: The side-gable duplex draws on late-19th-century American vernacular architecture, notably settlers' houses with the facade on the long wall and the roof ridge parallel to the street. It nonetheless incorporates the new standardised elements and materials that industrialisation in North America made it possible to produce on a large scale; the presence of sawmills in Hull eased access to lumber and drove the proliferation of the type, which also adopted a new structural system, balloon framing, itself made possible by the standardisation of lumber. Its apparently semi-detached spatial configuration answered a demand for rationalising space in urban settings, particularly in the very dense context of the working-class districts where the type is found. It appeared in Gatineau at the beginning of the 20th century, when urbanisation was being driven by strong labour demand tied to rapid industrialisation.

blurb_en: A rectangular house set broadside to the street under a straight gable roof of medium pitch, with one gable rising at the centre of the front — narrow on some houses, wide on others. The front is symmetrical: a central door, frequently with a transom and/or sidelights, a window to either side, and a window in the central gable.
origin_en: The central-gable house is among the first residential building types to take hold in the Hull region, from the 1830s, and was built throughout the 19th century, drawing on architectural elements characteristic of several styles. It is associated with Ontario vernacular architecture because of its strong popularity in the rural communities of Upper Canada, chiefly in the corridor between Kingston and Ottawa, where many pre-1860 examples are built of stone. In Québec it is often found in the anglophone communities of the south of the province; it also became a variant of the American industrial-influence house, made possible by the standardisation of materials, and spread to the other regions of Québec, notably the Gaspésie and the Maritimes, with often simplified ornamentation. The neo-Gothic features sometimes associated with the type — pointed-arch openings, wooden cladding, worked bargeboards, a finial crowning the gable dormer — are not present in Gatineau, where the type owes more to the Georgian style: rectangular plan, stone cladding, symmetrical composition, front gable, and a central door surmounted by a fanlight transom and framed by narrow sidelights.

blurb_en: Two and a half storeys under a roof the fiche itself calls complex: four slopes with hipped ends and projecting gables (frequent), two slopes with perpendicular gables, or a mansard with a projecting gable. The plan is rectangular, L-shaped or complex and throws off projections — a covered gallery on one or two façades, a pedimented porch, oriels, dormers — with a corner tower or turret under a cone, finial or dome on some of them.
origin_en: The type corresponds to the neo-Queen Anne style, which appeared in England in the middle of the 19th century, combining a taste for the picturesque inherited from the medieval era with the vocabulary of classical architecture. Named and popularised by a group of British architects, the most eminent of whom was Richard Norman Shaw, the style found imitators in the United States a decade later, in the 1870s, where it was adopted by the bourgeoisie, particularly in rural settings, whose large verandas, corner towers and numerous projections let owners enjoy the bucolic surroundings; unlike English houses, the structures and façades of American neo-Queen Anne houses used more wood. From the 1880s the style gained popularity in the United States and Canada thanks to the distribution of architectural catalogues, which let people easily order house plans — and the many prefabricated ornaments that make up these façades — by mail. In Quebec, the maison à toit complexe à pignon, drawing on the neo-Queen Anne style, was in vogue towards the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century.

origin_en: In Gatineau this type shares several characteristics with the maison allumette, the two kinds of dwelling having appeared at close periods; its layout may have been influenced by the narrowness of lots across the Gatineau territory. The two-slope mansard was popularised in Quebec after achieving great success in the United States from the 1850s onward, and houses built with this kind of roof took their inspiration at the time from Dutch houses. origin_en: The "maison allumette" appears from the 1870s, its origin owing notably to the opening of the American market to Canada; commercial and cultural exchange between the two countries brought in American architectural catalogues with illustrated plans and building instructions for wooden workers' houses, very popular with Canadian contractors and amateur builders. origin_en: The cubic house became popular at the start of the 20th century through the American architectural plan catalogues, which also enjoyed great success in Canada; from the 1890s those magazines published cubic-house plans, and by the 1900s the type had become a staple. Residential construction was democratising at the same time, eased by the arrival of standardised, machine-made building materials and architectural components ; the type is moreover associated with industrial vernacular architecture. Beyond the timbers of the structure and frame, the standardised and prefabricated elements turn up notably in the exterior and interior ornamentation, and that variety of ornaments and claddings also let the cubic house take on different architectural styles. Its popularity owed as well to the generous dimensions allowed by a square plan on two storeys, giving increased living space; industrialisation and the fall in construction costs it brought made the cubic house an affordable model.

Found in the Gatineau sector and particularly inside the site patrimonial du Quartier-du-Moulin, whose citation lists the setback from the street and the double row of pavement trees among the elements it protects.
origin_en: Built at the end of the 1920s, these houses were intended to lodge the executives of the Canadian International Paper (CIP), whose mill stood adjacent to — and gave its name to — the Quartier-du-Moulin. The building type belongs to the American Arts & Crafts current, whose stylistic and architectural characteristics were imported from the United Kingdom and adapted to the North American continent, and which favours natural materials such as wood in the form of shingles or boards, brick, or stone. Architectural magazines presenting house models were hugely popular in the United States and Canada in the early 20th century and spread the Arts & Crafts style through the anglophone world; the Toronto architect William Lyon Somerville, one of CIP's retained architects and the presumed designer of these houses, probably chose this style for the Quartier-du-Moulin residences. The movement's founding principles — the ideal of a return to nature and the appeal of a pastoral way of life — suited the garden-city principles the company followed in planning its towns, and details such as the roof coyaux and shed dormers found on some houses may vaguely evoke a thatched roof.

blurb_en: Two storeys under a flat roof, or a low slope falling to the rear, most often on a rectangular plan set perpendicular to the street. A porch (frequent) or covered gallery (occasional) stands at the front under a shed roof on wood columns, square more often than round; the simple main door, with a window beside it, is set off-centre. The sober ornament is concentrated on the roof overhang and the openings.
origin_en: Like most houses of the industrial vernacular style, the flat-roofed wood house appeared in the wake of industrialisation and the standardisation of building materials: milling lumber into studs of various dimensions (2" × 4", 2" × 6", etc.) made new techniques possible, notably wood-frame construction from the 1860s. Building this way was faster and cheaper and produced roomier houses, of two full storeys, within reach of the working class. The type is bound to industrialisation not only through its standardised materials and the new techniques that produced it, but through its purpose — housing a factory workforce newly settled in the cities, from the end of the 19th century into the beginning of the 20th — which is why most of these houses are found in dense urban settings. In the United States the type is often associated with the Boomtown style, which developed spectacularly at the time of industrialisation.

blurb_en: The brick counterpart of the wood flat-roofed house, and generally built later: two to three storeys of fine-grained red Modular brick in stretcher bond under a roof that is flat or falls gently to the rear. The street front is finished by a cornice with moulding carrying consoles, modillions or dentils, rarely with a parapet above; soldier courses run over the openings, or less often arched brick or moulded-concrete lintels, with moulded-concrete sills beneath the windows.
origin_en: The type follows the industrialisation of building materials and methods: Balloon Frame construction (charpente à claire-voie) arrived at the end of the 19th century and allowed faster building with standardised parts such as wood studs, while the waterproof roof membranes of the 1910s and 1920s permitted shallower roof slopes for drainage. It is often associated with the headlong growth of industrial zones in North American cities and of the workers' quarters near them. In Hull, sawmills made standardised wood easier to obtain, and ornamental elements in wood or metal, such as corbels, could be standardised too. Recourse to brick masonry as a cladding material became general after a by-law required incombustible cladding on buildings within the perimeter ravaged by the great Hull fire of 1900, so most flat-roofed brick houses in Gatineau were built after those of the same type in wood.

blurb_en: Two wings meeting at a right angle under a straight two-slope roof of medium to steep pitch. A covered gallery on one or two façades is frequent, commonly on worked columns; in rural settings it is often set into the crook of the L. Walls are usually wood clapboard or rabbeted board, sometimes red Modular brick. Some of these houses carry two entrance doors, one to each main volume.
origin_en: The L-plan house with a two-slope roof appears toward the end of the 19th century, when industrialisation made possible the mass production of standardised building materials, many of them in wood. Architectural and ornamental wood elements such as doors and windows were also available by catalogue, which gave the chance to personalise different types of houses, and the plans of these houses — the L-plan among them — were themselves available by catalogue. The period corresponds to a major development of North American cities, where demand for housing intensified because of the rural exodus. Though present in urban settings, the L-plan house also spread in rural areas in the context of settlement of the territory. The perpendicular arrangement of the two building volumes gives a spacious volume, less compact than a rectangular or cubic plan, it also allows a gallery to be inserted in the crook of the L, particularly observable in rural settings, and the numerous exterior walls that permit windows offering different views.

What the inventory calls a "version populaire et modeste" of the monumental style keeps only the mansard itself — the shallow terrasson above, the near-vertical brisis below, dormers punched through it — and the silhouette that villagers evidently liked.

The maison à mansarde is its domestic descendant: the roof survives, the avant-corps and the turret mostly do not. On this island it is common enough that the inventory calls the whole courant well represented.

blurb_en: The one courant on the island defined by refusing a rule. Plan asymmetrical, volume broken into projections, roof irregular and full of gables and turrets, several materials and colours at once, and no typical window. The inventory admits there are very few real examples here — mostly it is ordinary house types wearing an extraordinary decor.
origin_en: Québec architecture arrives at eclecticism toward the end of the 19th century, "un peu en réaction aux compositions rigides du classicisme", fusing borrowed elements from different periods and countries rather than reproducing any of them. Mechanised construction around 1880 made ornament cheap and fast, which is why façades carry so much of it. The movement runs roughly 1880–1920 in Québec and is called Victorian for Victoria's reign (1837–1901); for this current, "chaque œuvre est unique en soi".

massing: Rectangular volume showing a simplification of form. | A 1½-storey plank carré under a straight two-slope roof at 45° or with half-hips; the two-storey low-pitch model is also widespread. | Sub-variants: the cottage with half-hipped roof and the cottage with a gable dormer, otherwise identical.
articulation: Ornament drawn from the 19th-century repertoire but standardised and bought in: chambranles, planches cornières, aisseliers, frontons.
openings: Machined doors and windows — casement with transom, or sash.
materials: Light claddings: wood boards, asbestos-cement shingle, roughcast. | Gallery under an independent awning, often present.
courant: courant architectural (MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans inventory, 11 courants)
blurb_en: The traditional Québec house rebuilt out of a catalogue. The inventory is precise about the difference: this one rises to 1½ or 2 storeys instead of one and a half, which gives it more verticality, and its two straight slopes at 45° have no curved larmier. The symmetry survives; the carpentry does not.
origin_en: American vernacular architecture, the inventory says, is not a style at all — "elle reprend souvent les formes du siècle précédent en les simplifiant". What is new is the supply chain: milled beams and boards, doors and windows standardised and sold by catalogue, and the balloon frame (charpente claire) that made building fast and let a standard plan be fitted to a client's means. On this island the courant is thin, but it appears in nearly every municipality.
photo_credit: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 37 — six captioned examples, including a large gallery example and a gable-dormer variant, at Saint-Jean, Sainte-Pétronille, Sainte-Famille and Saint-Laurent. © Patri-Arch; rights ceded to the MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans. phase_title: Catalogue types — vernaculaire américain, cubique, Boomtown, Arts and Crafts
source_ref: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 42
source_generation: Patri-Arch inventory synthesis (cover Août 2014, fieldwork 2013–14, reissued 2025 as …maj2025.pdf), "Principaux éléments caractéristiques"
style_label: Arts and Crafts / Arts & métiers (Québec usage for Arts and Crafts)
siting_landscape: "Il existe peu d'exemples de ce style dans le site patrimonial de l'Île-d'Orléans et ils sont principalement situés à Sainte-Pétronille." | The inventory restricts the current to domestic and villégiature architecture only.
massing: A more or less imposing volume on an articulated plan — simple volumes distributed freely. | Roofs of varied form, with slopes or half-hips sometimes of unequal length, the larmier often projecting well past the façades.
articulation: Ornament often limited to members of the frame: colombage, exposed rafters, gallery supports. | "Chaque cas est unique et possède ses propres caractéristiques."
openings: Numerous and varied openings, with paired windows and hipped, lean-to or triangular dormers.
materials: Natural and traditional materials — stone, brick, stucco, cedar shingle, wood boards — sometimes combined. | Sheltered outdoor spaces: perrons, galleries, terraces.
courant: courant architectural (MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans inventory, 11 courants)
blurb_en: A house that breaks into wings and sheltered outdoor rooms under big overhanging roofs, with the structure itself doing the decorating — half-timbering, rafter ends carried out beyond the eaves, worked gallery posts. The inventory declines to generalise further, and says so: every case is its own.
origin_en: The English Arts and Crafts movement, rooted in Morris and Ruskin, argued for handwork, traditional materials and local skill against mass production. Crossing to the United States it lost the argument and kept the look: "en Amérique, le mouvement Arts and Crafts devient essentiellement un mouvement stylistique, sans portée sociale" — false half-timbering and slate roofs belonging to no local tradition, distributed by catalogue. On this island it is a Sainte-Pétronille resort style, and its best examples are the house and studio of the painter Horatio Walker.
photo_credit: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 43 — six captioned examples, all at Sainte-Pétronille, led by the maison and studio d'Horatio-Walker at 11 and 13 chemin Horatio-Walker. © Patri-Arch; rights ceded to the MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans. Not reproduced here.

source_generation: Patri-Arch inventory synthesis (cover Août 2014, fieldwork 2013–14, reissued 2025 as …maj2025.pdf), "Principaux éléments caractéristiques"
roofing: flat or low slope to the rear
siting_landscape: "Sur le territoire du site patrimonial de l'Île-d'Orléans, on retrouve quelques exemplaires de maisons Boomtown dans toutes les municipalités." | Both a domestic and a commercial current: "il n'est pas rare de retrouver un commerce au rez-de-chaussée avec un logement à l'étage".
massing: Cubic or rectangular two-storey volume, barely raised off the ground. | Flat roof, or a slight slope draining to the rear.
articulation: Ornament concentrated at the top of the façade: a modillon or console cornice, a stepped parapet, or brick patterning. | Other ornament stays discreet — chambranles, planches cornières, brick platebandes.
openings: Regular distribution of openings, generally symmetrical. | Casement windows with large panes, casement with transom, or sash.
