blurb_en: A flat-topped two-storey box that spends all its ornament in one place — the top of the front wall, where a bracketed cornice or a stepped parapet makes the building look taller and squarer than it is. Everything below that is plain boards or brick and a gallery.
origin_en: The balloon frame, "qualifiée d'American Boomtown", arrived with the fast growth of American cities and spread especially after the economic crisis of 1870 as a cheap, quick way to build in boom towns. In Québec it coexists with the traditional and mansard houses before supplanting them at the turn of the 20th century. On this island it never supplanted anything, but there are examples in all six municipalities.
photo_credit: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 41 — six captioned examples, including stepped-parapet houses at 504 and 1913 chemin Royal and a shop-house at 148 chemin du Bout-de-l'Île. © Patri-Arch; rights ceded to the MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans. Not reproduced here.

phase_title: Catalogue types — vernaculaire américain, cubique, Boomtown, Arts and Crafts
source_ref: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 38
source_generation: Patri-Arch inventory synthesis (cover Août 2014, fieldwork 2013–14, reissued 2025 as …maj2025.pdf), "Principaux éléments caractéristiques"
siting_landscape: "La maison cubique est assez peu représentée dans le site patrimonial de l'Île-d'Orléans." | A rural echo of an urban phenomenon: standardisation drove growth in the towns first, "ce phénomène se répercutera ensuite dans les milieux ruraux".
massing: Cubic volume on a square plan of two full storeys, raised slightly off the ground. | Low-pitch pavilion (four-slope) roof, sometimes flat; usually a dormer on the front slope.
articulation: "Ornementation variable selon le statut social du propriétaire" — the one type whose decoration the inventory ties explicitly to the owner's standing. | Picturesque influences show up on some models: aisseliers, ornamental woodwork, cornices.
openings: Regular distribution of openings. | Casement windows with large panes, casement with transom, or sash; hipped, gable, triangular or lean-to dormers, sometimes replaced by gables.
materials: Brick, or light cladding: wood boards, cedar shingle, embossed tin, asbestos-cement tile. | Gallery under an independent awning across the front, sometimes with a balcony above.
courant: courant architectural (MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans inventory, 11 courants)
blurb_en: Two entire floors under a shallow pavilion roof, on a square plan — a shape whose whole point is interior volume. The inventory says as much: its interest "réside dans les dimensions de son espace habitable", giving an ordinary family the room of a bourgeois house. How much ornament it carries depended on who was paying.
origin_en: An American model, "conçu par l'architecte Frank Kidder en 1891" and commonly called the Four Square house, spread through catalogues and trade journals across North America. It reached Québec's towns on the back of cheap standardised materials and falling construction costs, then reached the countryside. On Île d'Orléans it stayed rare.
photo_credit: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 39 — six captioned examples at Saint-Pierre, Saint-François, Saint-Jean and Sainte-Famille, including a brick example at 1634 chemin Royal. © Patri-Arch; rights ceded to the MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans. Not reproduced here.

phase_title: The bridge, régionalisme and modernisme
source_ref: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 46
source_generation: Patri-Arch inventory synthesis (cover Août 2014, fieldwork 2013–14, reissued 2025 as …maj2025.pdf), "Principaux éléments caractéristiques"
siting_landscape: "À l'île d'Orléans, nous n'avons répertorié qu'une résidence issue de l'architecture moderne." One house, out of 659. | The inventory names it: the maison Paul-Brunet, 37 chemin de l'Église, "témoigne de l'architecture moderne. Son architecture s'inspire notamment d'un paquebot."
massing: Simple volume, stripped of ornament. | Free plans producing very varied forms. | Flat roofs, or roofs of sculptural form.
articulation: No applied ornament: "l'expressivité des matériaux remplace les éléments d'ornementation".
openings: Large glazed surfaces, including horizontal ribbon windows.
materials: Modern materials — concrete and steel.
courant: courant architectural (MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans inventory, 11 courants)
blurb_en: The island's single modern house. The courant is a real one — free plan, flat or sculptural roof, concrete and steel, ribbon glazing, no ornament at all because the materials are the ornament — but on Île d'Orléans the inventory found exactly one example of it, and even that one is a ship: the maison Paul-Brunet at 37 chemin de l'Église, modelled on an ocean liner.
origin_en: Born of the European modern movement (Art nouveau, the Bauhaus) and American rationalism (the Chicago School), modernism breaks with inherited form more completely than any style before it — practical and functionalist, sober, refusing ornament, and putting aluminium, concrete, steel and large sheets of glass at the front of the design. It divides into several currents more or less faithful to the movement that produced them. Almost none of that reached this island.
photo_credit: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 46 — one captioned example, printed inline below the characteristics list: the maison Paul-Brunet at 37 chemin de l'Église. © Patri-Arch; rights ceded to the MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans. Not reproduced here.

phase_title: The bridge, régionalisme and modernisme
source_ref: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 44
source_generation: Patri-Arch inventory synthesis (cover Août 2014, fieldwork 2013–14, reissued 2025 as …maj2025.pdf), "Principaux éléments caractéristiques"
siting_landscape: "On ne retrouve que quelques cas de régionalisme québécois dans l'inventaire, surtout situé à Sainte-Pétronille, car cette architecture s'allie bien à celle de la villégiature." | The inventory warns that these houses are easy to misdate: "ces maisons peuvent souvent se confondre avec des constructions plus anciennes vue l'intention de les imiter".
massing: Rectangular volume, more or less imposing, with annexes. | High pitched roof, its slopes generally straight or slightly upturned, covered in wood or asphalt shingle.
articulation: Ornament often limited to the frames of the openings: chambranles, faux volets. | Sheltered outdoor spaces — perrons, galleries.
openings: Sash or casement windows with small panes, and generously sized gable dormers.
materials: Wood cladding — shingle or boards — or asbestos-cement. | Chimneys of massive appearance.
courant: courant architectural (MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans inventory, 11 courants)
blurb_en: A 1930s house built to look like a 1730s one. Québec's own version of Arts and Crafts went back to the buildings of the French regime for its vocabulary — high shingled roof, fire-break gable walls, stone or stucco standing in for lime — and copied them as faithfully as it could. On this island the results sit among the resort houses at Sainte-Pétronille, and the inventory dates the individual examples: 1939, 1940, 1944, 1945.
origin_en: "Le Québec possède une version du courant Arts and Crafts qui lui est propre, soit le régionalisme québécois", running from 1910 to the end of the Second World War. It began in the research of the McGill architecture professors Percy Erskine Nobbs and Ramsay Traquair, who wanted an authentically regional style, and spread through their students. It fed on the identity politics of the 1920s onward, which glorified New France, and found fertile ground under Duplessis; Gérard Morisset, the abbé Jean-Thomas Nadeau and Marius Barbeau argued for the same rediscovery of tradition.
photo_credit: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 45 — six captioned and dated examples — 1939, c. 1940, 1940, 1944 and 1945 — four of them at Sainte-Pétronille. © Patri-Arch; rights ceded to the MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans. Not reproduced here.

phase_title: Seigneurial côtes and the fur-trade posts
name_en: Stone house of the French tradition
name_fr: La maison de pierre de tradition française
source_ref: Répertoire du patrimoine culturel du Québec, fiches 93274 (site patrimonial Le Ber-Le Moyne, Lachine), 93440 (maison Rangé-dit-Laviolette, Baie-D'Urfé) et 92796 (maison Hyacinthe-Jamme-dit-Carrière, Pointe-Claire); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissements de Lachine, de Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé et de Pointe-Claire (2005)
source_generation: three RPCQ statements of heritage value (valeur patrimoniale + éléments caractéristiques) read against three sector-characterisation cahiers; no source publishes a per-type table for any West Island place, so the five columns are assembled from the three classed or cited houses themselves
roofing: cedar shingle at Le Ber-Le Moyne; ribbed copper sheet at Pointe-Claire today, over an original wood shingle
siting_landscape: Each of the three survivors sits on ground that predates the street grid around it. Le Ber-Le Moyne stands on a raised point of land beside lac Saint-Louis at the head of the Lachine rapids, on a slight mound planted with mature trees. | The Baie-D'Urfé house stands at the back of its lot, about a hundred metres from the public road and close to the shore, its main front turned south to the lake and the îles Sainte-Geneviève — RPCQ reads that orientation as evidence that the chemin du Roy once ran between the house and the water. | Pointe-Claire's house stands at the far end of a large treed lot that now isolates it from the postwar subdivision around it, on a censive conceded by the Sulpicians in 1722 along the côte Saint-Jean.
massing: A low stone carré on a near-square or short rectangular plan, one and a half storeys, sitting close to the ground. The Baie-D'Urfé carré measures 9.4 by 9.3 m. | Steep two-slope roof with straight slopes. Eaves are shallow at Lachine, and carried out over a covered gallery at Baie-D'Urfé and Pointe-Claire — in both cases a nineteenth-century alteration, not an original feature. | Ancillary buildings belong to the type where they survive - Lachine keeps a stone dépendance of the same date, and an 1781 census records a house, a barn and a stable at Baie-D'Urfé.
articulation: Almost none in the original fabric. What ornament these houses carry — moulded wood chambranles, gable dormers, a neo-Gothic porch, a bell-cast eave — was added between about 1828 and 1874 to bring them up to date.
openings: Openings set out asymmetrically, which RPCQ names as a French-tradition trait at both Baie-D'Urfé and Pointe-Claire. | Casement windows with small panes. At Pointe-Claire the south front is opened up for light while the north wall carries only two windows.
materials: Fieldstone throughout, laid up rubble. Pointe-Claire is left bare, and RPCQ names the absence of crépi as a Montréal-region trait; Baie-D'Urfé is whitewashed on three sides. | Two chimney stacks carried up in the line of the gable walls — the trait RPCQ singles out as belonging "plus particulièrement" to the houses of the island of Montréal and its neighbouring regions.
conservation: All three houses are protected individually, and none of the three village or shore ensembles around them is. Lachine's is a classed site patrimonial (2001) covering the exteriors and the land; Pointe-Claire's is a classed immeuble patrimonial (1964-08-12) covering exterior, interior and land; Baie-D'Urfé's is a municipal citation (2001) covering only the exterior envelope of the oldest, eastern section.
blurb_en: A low fieldstone box of one and a half storeys under a steep two-slope roof, stacks rising inside the gable walls, openings placed where they were wanted rather than where symmetry asked for them. Three of them survive across three of the six West Island places — a trading post of 1669–71 at Lachine, a farm house of about 1700 at Baie-D'Urfé, and one of 1769–91 at Pointe-Claire — and all three are protected individually while nothing around them is. One record, three municipalities: the photograph on this card is Lachine's, and Baie-D'Urfé's and Pointe-Claire's stand beside it on the type page.
origin_en: The Sulpicians became seigneurs of the island of Montréal in 1663 and conceded the côtes that run out to its western end; the houses built on those concessions were stone because stone was what the fields gave up and because fire and raiding made anything else a poor bet. What survives is very little. Lachine's is the oldest and least altered: two rectangular stone buildings put up in 1669–71 as a fur-trade post for Charles Le Moyne and Jacques Le Ber, restored in the 1980s toward their seventeenth-century appearance and now the Musée de Lachine. Baie-D'Urfé's was built about 1700 by Hubert Rangé dit Laviolette on a concession he bought in 1695, and then quietly rebuilt by the Pilon family between 1839 and 1874 — the walls raised, the roof pitch eased off, moulded chambranles and projecting eaves added in what RPCQ calls a taste imported after the Conquest. Pointe-Claire's went up between 1769 and 1791 on a censive conceded in 1722, and was altered again in 1828. Read together the three make the point the West Island pages keep making: the form is one form across three municipalities, the protection is three separate individual instruments granted in 1964, 2001 and 2001, and not one of them protects an ensemble.
photo_credit: « Site historique Le Ber-Le Moyne, 1, chemin du Musée (Lachine) », photo Denis Tremblay, 2012-12-03, from the Flickr stream *Parcours riverain — Ville de Montréal*. phase_title: Suburbanisation and the merger
source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), § 1.2.2 « Les ensembles urbains d'intérêt » et secteurs 7.U.1 à 7.U.8 (Dorval), 5.U.2 et 5.U.3 (Pointe-Claire), 19.U.2 (Lachine), 2.U.2 et 2.U.4 (Pierrefonds-Senneville) et 2.E.4 (Senneville), avec le § 2 Historique de l'arrondissement de Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé
source_generation: five sector-characterisation cahiers of the same 2005 series, read together; the series created a category, Ensembles urbains d'intérêt, expressly to catch postwar suburban housing, and that category is the only per-type writing any West Island source does
siting_landscape: Detached on its own lot, set back from the street with side margins, and with parking in the front yard — the Lachine cahier's description of the same wave, and the one place any West Island source describes the siting rule rather than the building. | Cul-de-sac and crescent street patterns recur, sometimes with a planted median down a wide avenue, and Dorval's cahier ties the effect of every one of these sectors to mature trees on the properties rather than to the houses. | Built in small series from a short catalogue of models. Dorval's 7.U.5 is praised for using « un nombre relativement restreint de modèles » while letting the materials vary house to house; Lachine's 19.U.2 calls the catalogue of types on its territory « particulièrement impressionnant ». In Lachine the dominant form of that catalogue is not this one but the taller contractor's box known locally as the maison « Gameroff », which carries its own record on that page; what belongs here is the alignment of Californian-inspired bungalows the cahier singles out at the end of the 51e Avenue.
massing: One storey, plain-pied. The Dorval cahier repeats the phrase « bungalows de type plain-pied, toit pavillon, brique » for two separate sectors, 7.U.1 and 7.U.4, and treats it as the norm for the municipality from the 1940s–50s onward. | A hipped roof is the commonest form. Lachine records more variety in the same years — pitched, hipped, or hipped combined with a false mansard. | Split-level versions appear in the same wave and the same decade; Dorval's 7.U.5 dates a whole quadrilateral of them to the 1950s.
articulation: Almost none, and what there is varies within a single street rather than between streets. Dorval's Model Homes are described as houses that look alike until you look closely, at which point the window types, the roofs, the use of artificial stone and clapboard and the handling of the brick are all different.
openings: Not described by any West Island source beyond the note that window types differ between otherwise identical Dorval houses.
materials: Brick dominant, with artificial stone and clapboard used as accent — the three materials Dorval's cahier names on avenue Dahlia. | Red brick at Pointe-Claire's Magil project, built 1953–55.
conservation: This is the only wave in the West Island whose recognition is explicitly experimental. The 2005 series says its own identification of these sectors « est exploratoire » and aims to link them to conservation concerns « pour une première fois ». | Where the cahiers return to it, they say the same thing twice - the value lies in the plan, the planting and the consistency of the materials rather than in any individual house, and personalisation is what erodes it. Lachine's 19.U.2 records that practically every building in its sector has been modified, and lists how: raising, building to the lot line, added upper storeys or a garage, changed cladding, changed openings, changed roof form. | Pointe-Claire's veterans' sector is the sharpest case: the cahier says few of the wartime houses are left and that what still marks the sector is the street layout and the subdivision, not the buildings.
blurb_en: One storey, hipped roof, brick with artificial stone and clapboard for variety, a carport or a garage, a cul-de-sac and mature trees. Built from a short catalogue of models across all six West Island places from the late 1940s, and the only twentieth-century housing the 2005 evaluation series took seriously enough to invent a category for.
origin_en: The wave arrives at different moments and for different reasons. At Dorval it is the airport: the aerodrome opened in 1941, air traffic grew fast after the war, the rest of the territory was opened to subdivision and the population went from under 3,000 in the 1940s to more than 20,000 by 1971. At Pointe-Claire it is a straight housing shortage — a veterans' sector on the Wartime Housing Limited model about 1947, then the Magil project of 1953–55. At Lachine it is what the cahier calls « l'urbanisation massive des années 1950-1970 », running east across the last open ground and producing a catalogue of contractors' types so consistent that the dominant one is still known locally by its builder's name. At Baie-D'Urfé it is the Métropolitaine and the demographic boom together, pushing settlement north across the railway for the first time. What the 2005 cahiers do with all of it is the interesting part. The series invented a category, Ensembles urbains d'intérêt, to hold postwar suburbs, said openly that the exercise was exploratory, and then valued these places for their street layouts, their planting and the consistency of their materials rather than for their architecture — while recording, in the same paragraphs, that almost every house had already been raised, extended, re-clad or re-roofed. It is the one wave on these six pages that the source treats as heritage-in-progress rather than as heritage.
photo_credit: The only photographs of West Island postwar bungalows located during this research are the 2005 Ville de Montréal évaluation cahiers' own — Dorval, p. 30–31, captioned « 7.U.1 165, rue McNicoll », « 7.U.2 1, avenue Dalhia », « 7.U.3 70, avenue des Lilas », « 7.U.4 Vue d'ensemble » and « 7.U.6 Avenue Claude »; Pointe-Claire, p. 34, « 5.U.2 Le 105 de l'avenue de Windward Crescent »; Lachine, p. 40, « 19.U.2 La 53e Avenue » and « 19.U.2 Une maison "Gameroff" typique au 3, 40e avenue ». © Ville de Montréal; not reproduced here. Wikimedia Commons was searched for a freely licensed photograph of a postwar bungalow in any of the six places and none was found. The one candidate that looked promising by its address — « Quatre-Vents, 12, avenue Dahlia (Dorval) », on the Model Homes street itself — was downloaded and inspected and is not a bungalow at all but a two-and-a-half-storey stuccoed house with a tiled coping and an arcaded loggia, so it was rejected. The Cité de Dorval's own heritage study of that address (LEMAYMICHAUD + Réal Paul architecte, « Expertise historique et étude patrimoniale, 12, avenue Dahlia, Dorval ») confirms the rejection and dates the house to 1803, enlarged 1874–85 in a neo-Gothic manner and wholly remade 1927–37 into the Italianate it wears now — one of the first stone houses in the district, standing on the street the bungalows were later built along, and not one of them. The same study independently repeats the cahier's figures for the 1951 project - 28 dwellings, 12 detached and 16 semi-detached bungalows, and two apartment buildings.

phase_title: The railway, the resorts and the country estates
name_en: Bourgeois brick house in the Victorian taste
name_fr: Maison bourgeoise en brique au goût victorien
source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Lachine (2005), sectors 19.I.2, 19.I.6, 19.I.7
source_generation: Sector characterisation. Three separate sector paragraphs name the same class of house; the record is their intersection and nothing more.
siting_landscape: On the boulevard Saint-Joseph between the 18th and 34th Avenues, where the cahier says the finest examples stand. | On the chemin de LaSalle and rue McLaughlin, in a sector the cahier reads as having a village atmosphere produced by low density and regular siting, with back gardens giving directly onto Lac Saint-Louis and open views between the buildings. | In the Saint-Antoine – Remembrance sector, where mature vegetation harmonises a mix of domestic and institutional building.
massing: The cahier gives no storey count. In Saint-Antoine – Remembrance it speaks of « belles séries d'habitations à la volumétrie plus ou moins complexe » — runs of houses of more or less complex massing — and that is the whole of what it says about volume. | Semi-detached as well as detached: « de belles maisons en brique jumelées d'inspiration victorienne ».
articulation: The word the cahier repeats is « cossues » — opulent — set against the modest small-gabarit architecture around them.
openings: The cahier states nothing about the openings of this type.
materials: Brick, in all three sectors.
blurb_en: The house of the people who did well out of the canal and the works: brick, opulent, Victorian in taste, detached or semi-detached, standing among much plainer neighbours on the boulevard Saint- Joseph, on the chemin de LaSalle and in the Saint-Antoine sector. The cahier calls it out three times and describes it none of them.
origin_en: The firms that came to the canal at the end of the 19th century employed more than labourers. What they built there is the beginning of the gradient this page is really about: worker housing east of the institutional core, bourgeois houses in the middle, and beyond the 32nd Avenue the summer-resort houses of Summerlea on their large treed lots, which belong to the shared West Island record for the villa anglaise de villégiature rather than here.

In the frame: a red-brick house with a round corner turret under a conical slate roof, gabled and dormered neighbours, and a lower stuccoed house with a columned porch. blurb_en: A small single-family house of one storey in brick, wider across the front than it is deep, finished at the top with a crown. It is the plainest thing in the old town and the cahier gives it eleven words; what those words describe is a house that is the mirror image of the Montréal shoebox, which turns its narrow end to the street and grows upward. origin_en: It belongs to the dense grid of Vieux-Lachine, which grew along the boulevard Saint-Joseph and then reached rue Saint-Louis and rue Victoria as the arrival of firms like Dominion Bridge consolidated Lachine's industrial vocation. The cahier sets it in a list beside the wooden village houses, the attached and terraced houses under mansards and false mansards, and the brick duplexes and triplexes — four kinds of small dwelling on the same street grid, housing the workforce that the canal and the factories drew in.

name_en: The maison « Gameroff » — contractor-built house of the 1950s–1970s quarters

massing: One or two storeys. | Square or rectangular plan, simple massing. | Roof forms vary: pitched, hipped, or a hipped-and-false-mansard combination.
articulation: Decorative elements in wood on a brick wall, and nothing else the cahier records. | Practically every building in the sector has been modified and personalised: raised, built out to the lot line, given extra storeys or a garage, re-clad, re-fenestrated, re-roofed. blurb_en: A detached one- or two-storey house on a square or rectangular plan, simple in massing, clad in brick with wooden trim, under a roof that might be pitched, hipped, or hipped with a false mansard; set back from the street with side yards and a car parked in front, and built in small series. What makes it worth a card is its name. The cahier records that among the contractors who built the 1950s–1970s quarters of Lachine, the best known locally gave the dominant house type its familiar name — the maison « Gameroff » — and that is a piece of purely local vernacular naming that made it into a municipal heritage document.
origin_en: Lachine answered the postwar boom the way other towns did, by turning its unbuilt sectors into dormitory quarters, and the sector called Victoria – Sir-George-Simpson is what came out: a vast, very homogeneous stretch of detached houses that the cahier says testify to the emergence of a middle class, to individual ownership, and to a way of living made possible by the car. It also says the catalogue of types deployed there is "particulièrement impressionnant" and lists three at once — Boomtown houses, bungalows, and the contractors' houses of which the Gameroff is the dominant one. That is the note this record should end on: a document written to identify heritage found a 1950s–1970s tract worth naming as an ensemble, and named its houses after the man who built them.

phase_title: Longue-Pointe — the côtes, the redoubt and the village
name_fr: La maison villageoise de Longue-Pointe (maison en carré de bois)
source_ref: Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), sector 27.I.3 Longue-Pointe and ch. 2
siting_landscape: Along the old chemin du Roy — the present rue Notre-Dame Est — and the village streets running off it, around the parish church of Saint-François-d'Assise on the river bank; the church itself has been demolished. | The village core was « largement amputé » when the Louis-Hippolyte-Lafontaine bridge-tunnel was built in the early 1960s, so what survives is a fragment, not a continuous frontage.
massing: Small village gabarit, one to one-and-a-half occupied levels.
materials: Squared-timber walls — « maisons en carré de bois » — most often sheathed in wood boards or wood shingles, and sometimes in clay brick.
blurb_en: What was on the ground before any of the rest of it. Small squared-timber houses sheathed in board, shingle or brick, strung along the old chemin du Roy around a parish founded in 1722 — the oldest settlement layer in the borough, and the one most thoroughly cut apart, first by the tramway that reached the end of the island in 1897 and then by the bridge-tunnel approaches of the early 1960s.
origin_en: Longue-Pointe is the borough's French-regime layer. A wooden redoubt went up on the shore about 1670 in the chain of forts protecting Ville-Marie; a chapel and presbytery followed at the turn of the eighteenth century; Saint-François-d'Assise de la Longue Pointe became, in 1722, one of the few parishes erected on the island under the French regime, and the territory became a municipality in 1845. In 1825 the parish counted 67 houses, holding « de nombreux artisans, des aubergistes, des rentiers, des journaliers mais surtout des agriculteurs ». Its urbanisation came late precisely because it was far from Montréal's economy, and the cahier says so: development « se fera plus tardivement que celui des municipalités voisines (Hochelaga et Maisonneuve) puisqu'elle est située assez loin du centre des activités économiques de Montréal ». Longue-Pointe, Beaurivage and Tétraultville were all annexed to Montréal in 1910.

phase_title: Hochelaga industrialises and is annexed
name_en: Company workers' house of the Hudon mill, rue Saint-Germain
name_fr: La maison ouvrière de la filature Hudon, rue Saint-Germain
source_ref: MEM, « Les maisons ouvrières de la rue Saint-Germain » (2017); Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), sector 27.E.1
siting_landscape: Built at the sidewalk edge with no setback, and set in an unbroken run — « disposées en enfilade et en bordure du trottoir ». | Rue Saint-Germain between rues Rouville and Adam, civic numbers 1451 to 1544; one of the three streets sector 27.E.1 names as the first ground of Hochelaga's workers' housing.
massing: Square-ish two-storey volumes — « cubes de bois revêtus de briques ». | Two dwellings, one on the ground floor and one above, reached by a stair inside the building. No exterior stair; this is 1881, nearly twenty years before the outside stair becomes standard in Montréal.
materials: Wood frame faced in brick.
blurb_en: The corporate counterpart to Maisonneuve, built two years before Maisonneuve existed. Brick-faced wooden cubes running unbroken along the sidewalk on rue Saint-Germain, two dwellings each with the stair inside, put up in 1881 by the V. Hudon cotton mill for its own workers — and, according to the Ville's MEM, the only surviving nineteenth-century company-built housing in Montréal.
origin_en: Hochelaga industrialised faster than it could house anyone. Four large works arrived between 1871 and 1881 — the W.C. McDonald tobacco factory, the Abattoirs de l'Est, the Compagnie des moulins à coton V. Hudon and the Filature Sainte-Anne, the last two merging in 1905 into Dominion Textile, which then held half of the Canadian textile industry — and, in the Évaluation's words, « les terrains sont lotis sans réglementation particulière ». The Hudon mill announced its own workers' housing in early December 1881 and built this row; it was renovated in 1981, exactly a century later. Read this record against the plex on the next page and against Arvida and Témiscaming: an employer housing its workforce directly is what a company town does, and it is precisely what Maisonneuve two years later did not do. Maisonneuve's promoters sold lots and built civic monuments instead, and left the housing to the ordinary speculative builder.

phase_title: The cité de Maisonneuve
name_en: Bourgeois residence of the cité, Beaux-Arts
source_ref: RPCQ fiche 92740, Château Dufresne; Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), ch. 2 and sector 27.E.3
siting_landscape: Set on a large landscaped ground behind a cast-iron fence, on one of the two thoroughfares laid out for prestige — rue Sherbrooke Est, or boulevard Pie-IX, whose subdivision « privilégiait de riches constructions sur des terrains plus grands que ce que l'on retrouve dans les environs ». | Garages and other service space put underground at the rear rather than on the street front.
massing: Rectangular two-storey corps de logis under a flat roof ringed by a balustrade. | Two paired houses composed as one unified block, with lateral wings set back from the main façade and rising only to half height, and a rear annex holding a winter garden.
articulation: Symmetry and frontality — two avant-corps framing a central section carried on three pairs of coupled Ionic columns. | Classical ornament — column capitals, entablature and the terrace roof edged with a balustrade. The RPCQ names this house, with the Maisonneuve bain public et gymnase and the Saint-Sulpice library, as an illustration of Beaux-Arts composition applied in Québec.
openings: Vertical rectangular and round-headed openings, disposed symmetrically about the central bay.
materials: Indiana limestone facing. | Structure and twenty massive piers in reinforced concrete.
blurb_en: The exception the record keeps insisting on. Two houses for two brothers built as one Beaux-Arts block in Indiana limestone — Marius Dufresne, who as municipal engineer designed Maisonneuve's public buildings, on one side, and Oscar Dufresne, who ran the family shoe factory, on the other — standing on twenty reinforced-concrete piers at a moment when almost no house in Montréal did. Forty rooms, a winter garden, garages underground.
origin_en: Maisonneuve was 80 % francophone and, in the Évaluation's phrase, « composée surtout de travailleurs et de locataires »; its promoters had founded the place in 1883 to be, as the RPCQ puts it, « la "Westmount des francophones" ». The bourgeois house is where that ambition became a building. The Dufresne brothers were both instruments of it: Oscar sat as échevin and ran Dufresne et Locke, the shoe manufactory established at Maisonneuve about 1900 and one of its largest employers; Marius was municipal engineer from 1910 to 1918 and drew the market (1912–1914), the fire station (1914–1915) and the public bath and gymnasium (1914–1916). They began their own house in 1915, the year the civic building programme was breaking the city's finances, and finished it in 1918, the year the province annexed Maisonneuve to Montréal. It was classé in 1976; the civic buildings had to wait until 2022.

phase_title: The cité de Maisonneuve
name_en: Shop-and-dwellings block on the commercial artery
name_fr: L'immeuble commercial avec logements, rues Ontario et Sainte-Catherine
source_ref: Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), sectors 27.E.2 and 27.I.1; Guide patrimonial de MHM
siting_landscape: Built to the lot lines with no setback, on the corner of a commercial artery and a residential street — rue Ontario Est and rue Sainte-Catherine Est are the two the Évaluation identifies as the axes of urban development once the tramway reached the east end. | The corner is chamfered so the shop entrance faces the crossing.
massing: Three storeys under a flat roof, shop at street level and dwellings above. | A projecting oriel rides the chamfered corner through the upper storeys.
articulation: Ground floor read as its own register — the borough's Guide patrimonial defines « entablement » precisely as « partie supérieure d'un rez-de-chaussée (commercial) prenant la forme d'un bandeau ». | Crown gathered into a bold projecting cornice of worked painted metal, ornamented across the whole frontage and returning around the chamfer.
openings: Vertical rectangular upper windows in regular bays; glazed shopfront below, here with glass-block infill of a later phase.
materials: Rock-faced grey limestone above, brick at the shopfront piers; the Guide's palette for significant sectors allows grey limestone, smooth or rock-faced, and clay brick in red, brown, beige, orange, polychrome or glazed.
blurb_en: The other half of Maisonneuve's zoning experiment. Where the by-law let commerce go — rue Ontario Est, rue Sainte-Catherine Est — the block turns its corner on a chamfer, puts a shop under three storeys of flats, runs an oriel up the angle and finishes the whole thing with an ornamented metal cornice. The streets the by-law reserved for housing got the plex instead, and no shop at all.
origin_en: The tramway is the cause. The Évaluation dates Hochelaga's commercial axes to the moment the streetcar arrived — rue Sainte-Catherine and the new Montreal Street Railway viaduct of 1892 « pour desservir les populations de l'est montréalais » — and dates Maisonneuve's own growth from the same year: « à partir de 1892, les tramways favorisent le développement rapide de Maisonneuve et placent la municipalité dans la zone d'influence de Montréal ». Shops followed the rails, and the corner block is what a builder puts on a lot that has to earn from both a shopfront and a stack of flats.

phase_title: The cité de Maisonneuve
name_fr: L'habitation ouvrière de trois étages (« plex »)
source_ref: Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), sector 27.E.2 and § 3.1; Guide patrimonial de MHM
siting_landscape: Continuous alignments along tree-lined streets — the Évaluation names the trees twice, in the sector fiche (« le long de rues bordées d'arbres ») and in its overview of the borough's residential heritage. | In Hochelaga the first such streets are Moreau, Dézéry and Saint-Germain, settled directly around the deep-water port and the Notre-Dame rail lines; in Maisonneuve the sector runs east to Viauville, between rues Sicard and Viau.
massing: Three storeys, one dwelling to a floor, under a flat roof. | Front balcony at each upper level, and an exterior stair climbing to the upper doors so that every dwelling keeps its own entrance from the street.
articulation: Crown treated as a distinct element — the borough's conservation guide governs « couronnement » as its own category, in worked and painted wood, worked painted metal, or brick laid in a distinctive bond, plus false mansards and dômes in natural slate, fish-scale metal or tôle à la canadienne. | Openings framed by a lintel of brick laid as a shallow-arched soldier course, of stone, or of concrete with a moulded relief, over a stone or concrete sill 5 to 6 inches high.
openings: Vertical openings; for pre-1940 buildings the guide prescribes double-hung sashes at 1/2–1/2 or 2/5–3/5, or casements at 1/3–2/3 or 2/5–3/5 with a fixed upper light, glazed in uniform clear or frosted glass without muntins or patterns. | Principal door with a glazed panel 42 to 54 inches high, and a secondary balcony door glazed 36 to 42 inches, which may carry the traditional Montréal muntin pattern.
materials: The Évaluation's own words for the borough's residential heritage — « plex » en pierre ou en brique. Grey limestone, smooth-faced or rock-faced, and clay brick in red, brown, beige, orange or polychrome, plus glazed brick. | Stair, balcony guard and stringer in steel, wrought iron or welded aluminium, painted; natural galvanised steel is prohibited as a non-original component. Balcony floors in tongue-and-groove wood or composite board, boards no wider than 6 inches, on a bipartite wooden fascia with a slatted wooden soffit.
blurb_en: What Maisonneuve's workers actually lived in. Three storeys of grey limestone or clay brick under a flat roof, one dwelling to a floor, each with its own door off the street and the upper doors reached by an iron stair curving up out of the front yard — repeated down both sides of a street planted with trees. The Évaluation gives it one clause and no fiche, which is the point: the ambition at Maisonneuve went into the civic buildings and the boulevard, and the housing was the standard Montréal product.
origin_en: The form arrives with the industry. Hochelaga's mills — the W.C. McDonald tobacco works, the Abattoirs de l'Est, the V. Hudon cotton mills and the Filature Sainte-Anne, all established between 1871 and 1881 — drew what the cahier calls « une main-d'œuvre bon marché issue des populations agricoles qui convergent vers la ville », and « les terrains sont lotis sans réglementation particulière ». At Maisonneuve after 1883 the promoters offered huge cheap lots and tax exemptions to industry, and the population went from about 350 at the founding to 2,000 in 1896 and roughly 18,000 in 1911 — 80 % francophone and « composée surtout de travailleurs et de locataires ». Renters in a boom is what the plex is for. Maisonneuve also enacted a zoning by-law that the cahier calls « une nouveauté à l'époque », barring shops and industry from certain streets reserved for housing alone — one of the earliest use-separation controls in Québec, and the reason these streets read as purely residential while rue Ontario Est a block away does not.

phase_title: Suburban Mercier — veterans' houses, bungalows, the Olympic Park
name_en: Brick bungalow of the 1950s Mercier developments
name_fr: Le bungalow de brique des lotissements de Mercier
source_ref: Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), sectors 27.U.2, 27.U.3 and 27.U.5
siting_landscape: Whole developments built to one plan, with rows of trees along the sidewalk that the cahier reads as deliberate — « les alignements d'arbres matures en bordure du trottoir, découlant d'un plan d'ensemble organisé, ajoutent à l'harmonie des rues ». | In the 1955 ensemble the streets run in loops, « le type de lotissement qui est popularisé dans les nouvelles banlieues développées après la guerre ».
massing: One storey. In the earliest ensemble (rues Honoré-Beaugrand to Cirier, early 1950s) a square plan with no door on the principal façade at all, only a band of windows set either to the left or to the right. | In the 1955 ensemble (rues Honoré-Beaugrand and Chénier), detached or semi-detached, rectangular or L-plan, hipped or gabled roofs, with or without a carport.
openings: A horizontal window band as the whole of the principal façade's composition, in the earliest ensemble.
materials: Brick throughout, and it stays dominant — in the 1955 ensemble most houses have taken on individuality through changed cladding or windows, « cependant, la plupart respectent leur volume et leur composition d'origine et la brique reste le matériau dominant ».
blurb_en: The other post-war Mercier, and the odder one. Identical brick bungalows put up in whole streets in the early 1950s — in one development with no front door at all on the street face, just a band of windows pushed to one side — laid out with rows of trees along the sidewalk that the Ville's surveyors could still recognise fifty years later as part of the original plan.
origin_en: Mercier is where the borough turned suburban. The Évaluation notes that the criteria it used to find heritage sectors « n'a pas permis d'identifier beaucoup de secteurs dans la partie est du territoire », and answers itself: « cela ne signifie pas pour autant que cette partie de l'arrondissement ne présente pas d'intérêt. Les qualités d'ensemble de plusieurs rues devraient être maintenues. » That is why these four developments are recorded as ensembles urbains d'intérêt rather than as heritage sectors — the value is in the coherence of a whole street, not in any single house, and the document's own recommendation is to study such territories, « recenser les typologies des ensembles qui présentent une grande homogénéité », and build public awareness of them. It is a recommendation for exactly the kind of record this page is.

phase_title: Suburban Mercier — veterans' houses, bungalows, the Olympic Park
name_en: Veterans' house, to the Wartime Housing Limited model
source_ref: Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), sectors 27.U.1 and 27.U.4; Guide patrimonial de MHM, « Maison des vétérans » types I–III
siting_landscape: Grouped as whole developments rather than as single houses, laid out to one plan; the borough's ensembles are north of rue de Rouen and along rue Curatteau.
massing: Detached houses of closely similar volume across the whole ensemble — « ces maisons présentent une volumétrie semblable, apportant une harmonie certaine à l'ensemble ». | Two-slope gabled roof. | The borough's Guide distinguishes three variants and notes that type II carries an entrance vestibule (« tambour d'entrée ») and therefore has no columns.
articulation: Guard rails 36 inches high; simple painted metal fascia; painted or natural wooden slat soffits; painted untreated wooden columns where there are any. | Wooden surround mouldings, painted and untreated, around the cladding.
openings: Double-hung windows in a 1/2–1/2 ratio, glazed in uniform clear or frosted glass without patterns, muntins permitted. | Door carrying one glazed panel, optionally divided into nine lights, the glass clear and plain, 91.4 to 124.5 cm high.
materials: Light horizontal wood clapboard in a pale, low-contrast tone harmonised with its surroundings; brick with a two-slope roof in the rue Curatteau ensemble. | Original roof covering is asphalt shingle — stated as such by the Guide for both the maisons des vétérans and the Village Champlain houses.
blurb_en: The federal minimal house, arriving in Mercier after the war it was invented for. A detached one-and-a-half-storey box under a two-slope roof, clad in pale clapboard or brick, built in whole streets to one volume so that the ensemble reads as a single gesture — around 1950 north of rue de Rouen, in 1953 on rue Curatteau.
origin_en: The Évaluation states the lineage exactly: these ensembles were built « autour de 1950 sur le modèle des maisons de la Wartime Housing Limited. Ce modèle a été développé durant la Deuxième Guerre mondiale pour répondre à la crise du logement qui sévissait alors et pour loger les ouvriers à proximité des entreprises consacrées à l'industrie de guerre. Le modèle fut adopté par la suite par plusieurs promoteurs qui cherchaient à rejoindre un segment de marché composé de personnes désirant habiter une maison individuelle à prix abordable. » That last clause is the whole post-war housing shift in one sentence: a state emergency type turned into a market product. The same object appears on this site at Lévis, in the Sud-Ouest, in Villeray–Saint-Michel–Parc-Extension, in Parc-Extension and at Verdun's Crawford Park; this is its eastern Montréal instance, and it is the one place in this borough where the cahier uses the word « modèle » of a house at all.
photo_credit: pending — the one Commons image of rue Curatteau was checked and rejected: it shows yellow-brick plexes at the north end of the street, not the 1953 gabled brick ensemble of sector 27.U.4

phase_title: Garden City and Montreal vernacular
source_ref: By-law 1449, art. 19
style_label: Arts and Crafts / English Domestic Revival
siting_landscape: At least 60 % of the front yard kept as vegetation | Side driveway, minimum width about 2.5 m | Narrow pedestrian path (curved or not), separate from the driveway | Front setback of about 14 m from the sidewalk; side setbacks of about 3.5 m | Typical lot width 10–12 m
massing: Fragmented volumes | Typical width of 7.5 m per semi-detached unit, 15 m for a detached house | Habitable attic storey | Projecting elements (balconies, entrance vestibules, verandas, solariums) may be altered if they still read as distinct from the main volume through a light cladding (wood, aluminium, composite or acrylic) and keep their high degree of openness | Detached garage, or one set back from the front façade so it reads as a separate volume
articulation: Multi-slope roofs, steeply pitched (45°), with gables | Asymmetrical composition
openings: Small-paned glazing | Bay windows may be added if they respect the type | Vertical window proportion (height = twice the width)
materials: Brownish-red clay brick on the ground floor, in a small traditional module (4 in. deep × 8 in. long × 2.5 in. high) | Stucco and/or wood half-timbering on the upper floor and in the gables | Dark asphalt shingle roofing | Same roofing material (texture and colour) on the main roof and on porch and gallery roofs | Wood balustrades and columns for balconies and galleries
blurb_en: The founding house type of TMR. When Frederick Todd laid out the town in 1912 he was borrowing directly from Ebenezer Howard's Garden City movement, and the first houses near the station borrowed the movement's architecture too: the English Arts-and-Crafts cottage of Letchworth and Hampstead Garden Suburb. Look for steep 45° gables, a brick ground floor with stucco or half-timbering above, small-paned windows, and a deliberately picturesque, asymmetrical silhouette that reads as a cottage in a garden rather than a house on a street.
origin_en: The Garden City movement's architecture as well as its planning. Ebenezer Howard's 1898 tract produced Letchworth (Parker & Unwin, 1903) and Hampstead Garden Suburb (1907), and their house vocabulary, itself drawn from Voysey, Baillie Scott and the English cottage, travelled with the idea: steep gables, roughcast or half-timbered upper storeys over brick, small-paned casements, picturesque asymmetry, the house read as a cottage in a garden. The by-law's Garden City House is this, with the 45° roof, stucco-and-timber upper floor and small brick module written out as criteria.

source_ref: By-law 1449, art. 20

blurb_en: “Faubourien” refers to the vernacular of Montreal's old inner suburbs (the faubourgs): a plain two-storey brick box, flat or hipped roof, sometimes a false mansard, and a front verandah on wooden columns. In TMR the type is what the Plateau or Rosemont row house becomes when it is given its own lot, a side driveway and a lawn. Its virtue is restraint: symmetry, aligned windows, one material.
origin_en: Faubourien points to the maison de faubourg, the plain brick house of Québec's nineteenth-century inner suburbs: two or three storeys, flat or false-mansard roof, aligned openings, minimal ornament, a front gallery on wooden posts. Montreal's Plateau PIIA uses the same term for its own housing stock. In TMR the type is what that urban house becomes on a detached or semi-detached lot with a side driveway; several examples take on the cubic mass and hipped roof of the American Foursquare, which was being built across Canada in the same years.

phase_title: Garden City and Montreal vernacular
source_ref: By-law 1449, art. 21
style_label: Interwar walk-up, with Art Deco and stripped-classical trim
siting_landscape: At least 95 % of the front yard kept as vegetation | Parking in a basement garage at the rear or side, reached from a lane
massing: Simple volumes | Position and visibility of the main entrances preserved
articulation: Base of the building differentiated from the upper floors by a specific treatment | A single building body crowned by a brick motif and a parapet | Aligned openings and symmetrical composition preserved | Balconies, with attention to railing detail | Entrances sheltered by a substantial portico
openings: Divided-light glazing | Bay windows may be added if they respect the type | Vertical window proportion maintained (height = twice the width) | Character of the wooden entrance doors and their glazing proportion preserved | Window frame colour coordinated with the facing brick

blurb_en: The interwar Montreal walk-up, three storeys of red brick under a flat roof, with a decorated parapet, a stone base, patterned brickwork and a prominent entrance portico. Balconies with iron or stone railings give the façade its rhythm. These sit on the town's few multi-family lots and are the collective sibling of the faubourg house.
origin_en: Three-storey brick apartment houses of the 1920s and 30s, Montreal's standard multi-family building of the period. This is where Art Deco actually lives in TMR: stepped and decorated parapets, geometric brick panels, artificial-stone entrance surrounds, iron balcony rails with angular motifs. Héritage Montréal describes the same repertoire on 1920s Montreal plexes (dark brick, artificial-stone insertions around doors and windows, appliqués with geometric forms). The by-law absorbs it as "distinctive brick motifs and bonds" and "a body crowned by a brick motif and a parapet" rather than naming the style.

phase_title: The period revivals
source_ref: By-law 1449, art. 22
siting_landscape: At least 60 % of the front yard kept as vegetation | Driveway of medium width | Narrow pedestrian path distinct from the driveway | Front setback of about 14 m from the sidewalk; side setbacks of about 3 m | Typical lot width 15–22 m
massing: Habitable attic storey | Main entrance sheltered by the roof's drip edge (larmier) | Attached garages | Garage volume and roof distinct from those of the main building | Typical width of 11 m per semi-detached unit, 15 m for a detached house

openings: Small-paned glazing | Bay windows may be added if they respect the type | Vertical window proportion (height = twice the width)
materials: Natural stone facing | Dark asphalt shingle roofing | Same roofing material on the main roof and on dormer roofs
blurb_en: A 1930s–50s revival of the 18th-century Quebec farmhouse: a steep roof whose eaves flare out into “larmiers” that shelter the front door, a row of dormers, fieldstone walls, and a calm symmetrical front. It was the domestic face of a broader interwar interest in Québécois heritage. The distinctive move is the roof, which is asked to express the base of the house through its overhang.
origin_en: A regionalist revival of the eighteenth-century Laurentian farmhouse: bell-cast roof whose eaves flare into larmiers sheltering the door, a row of dormers, fieldstone walls, a calm symmetrical front. The Canadian Encyclopedia locates its source in the anglophone rediscovery of pre-industrial Québec during the 1920s–30s, stimulated by Clarence Gagnon's paintings and encouraged by Percy Nobbs and Ramsay Traquair at McGill, whose surveys of old Québec buildings fed a fashion for fieldstone and pitched roofs among the province's leading domestic architects. TMR's Canadian houses are the suburban, builder-scale version of that fashion.

source_ref: By-law 1449, art. 23

blurb_en: Colonial Revival as it arrived from the American Northeast: a long, simple gabled rectangle with its broad side to the street, symmetrical windows, dormers set halfway up the roof, and a discreet canopy over the front door. Brick or stone below, clapboard or stucco above. It is quieter than the Georgian house, and the by-law wants it kept quiet: bay windows are the only projections allowed.
origin_en: A long side-gabled rectangle with its broad face to the street, symmetrical openings, dormers half-way up the roof, a discreet door canopy; brick or stone below and clapboard or stucco above. It is the New England colonial house as codified in 1920s–40s pattern books and builders' plan services, the quieter cousin of Georgian Revival. The by-law keeps it quiet: bay windows are the only projections it allows.

source_ref: By-law 1449, art. 24

blurb_en: Low-rise red-brick apartment courts arranged in U or L plans around a green forecourt, with steep gables, dormers and the occasional turret. A stone base and stone string courses tie them to the collegiate-Tudor mood of the interwar decades. Entrances are marked by a distinct architectural element rather than a big portico.
origin_en: Low-rise red-brick apartment blocks in U or L plans around a green forecourt, with stone bases, stone string courses, steep gables, dormers and the occasional turret. The idiom is the residential cousin of interwar school and college architecture, and of the "garden apartment" courts built across North America in the 1930s–40s. The by-law's "New England (collective)" label is looser than the architecture: these blocks are more Tudor than New England.

phase_title: The period revivals
source_ref: By-law 1449, art. 25

blurb_en: Georgian Revival: the most formal of TMR's houses. A red-brick box of two full storeys, three or five bays wide, with a central door flanked by pilasters and topped by an elaborate crown, sash windows with small panes, and a frieze under a moderately pitched hip or side-gabled roof. Symmetry is the whole point; the by-law lets you emphasise the central bay with a slight projection and a pediment, and nothing more.
origin_en: The formal wing of Colonial Revival. Two full storeys of red brick, three or five bays, a central door with pilasters and an entablature or pediment, sash windows with small panes, a frieze under a moderately pitched hip or side-gable roof. Symmetry is the whole point; the by-law permits one flourish, a slightly projected central bay under a pediment, and nothing else. In Canada the style carried an Imperial-loyalist inflection that made it a natural fit for a town founded and first settled by anglophones.

source_ref: By-law 1449, art. 26

blurb_en: Tudor Revival, TMR's most romantic type: steep 45° roofs broken into several gables, a natural-stone ground floor with brick or half-timbered stucco above, patterned brickwork (herringbone, Dutch bond), small-paned casements, sometimes a round turret at the entrance. Where the Georgian house is symmetrical, the manor is deliberately picturesque, and its garage is meant to hide.
origin_en: The by-law's "English manor" is Tudor Revival by any other name: stone ground floor with brick or stucco-and-timber above, patterned brick (herringbone, Dutch bond), 45° multi-gabled roofs, small-paned casements, sometimes a round entrance turret. In North America the style peaked in the 1920s–30s and lingered into the 1940s; its Montreal fashion was strongest in the anglophone west end and suburbs. Tudor detailing also surfaces on some Phase 1 Garden City houses, which is why the two types share the half-timbered gable.

source_ref: By-law 1449, art. 27

blurb_en: The postwar ranch bungalow: one storey, long and low, with a shallow-pitched roof whose overhang shelters a recessed door, a garage pushed forward into the façade, and big undivided windows wider than they are tall. Buff (“chamois”) brick or stone, black shingles, a wide driveway. The type that arrived with the car and the last empty lots of the 1950s and 60s.
origin_en: One storey, long and low, a shallow-pitched roof whose overhang shelters a recessed door, a garage pushed forward into the façade, big undivided windows wider than tall, buff ("chamois") brick or stone, a wide driveway. In Québec usage bungalow simply means the postwar single-family suburban house; the form is the Ranch house that spread from the American Southwest after 1945 and became the default Canadian suburban dwelling of the 1950s–60s.
photo_credit: © Ville de Mont-Royal, By-law 1449 art. 27

phase_title: Postwar suburban modern
source_ref: By-law 1449, art. 28
style_label: Postwar two-storey (Québec cottage), with Minimal Traditional and Moderne notes
siting_landscape: At least 60 % of the front yard kept as vegetation | Wide driveway | Pedestrian path joins the driveway | Front setback of about 12 m from the sidewalk; side setbacks of about 2.5 m | Typical lot width 20–25 m
massing: Simple volumes of two full storeys | Typical width of 15 m per semi-detached unit, 16 m for a detached house | Garage integrated into the volume, in the façade | Entrance sheltered by a marquise

materials: Natural stone or red clay brick on the ground floor | Stucco or clapboard on the upper floor | Black asphalt shingles, or a tone matched to the cladding colour
blurb_en: In Quebec usage a “cottage” is simply a two-storey detached house, and this is its postwar version: a plain box under a low hip roof, stone or brick on the ground floor with stucco or siding above, garage built into the front, and a flat marquise over the door. A visible line at the ground-floor lintels or the upper sills divides base from body.
origin_en: In Québec real-estate usage a cottage is a two-storey detached house, as opposed to the one-storey bungalow; the OQLF notes the word's British origin and its earlier sense of an elegant, English-inspired country house. TMR's postwar cottage is a plain box: stone or brick base, stucco or siding above, low hip roof, integrated garage, flat marquise over the door, a horizontal line at the ground-floor lintels or upper sills dividing base from body. Some examples keep vestigial colonial detailing (Minimal Traditional); others, in cut stone with flat roofs and rounded or banded corners, are the town's clearest echo of Streamline Moderne.

source_ref: By-law 1449, art. 29

blurb_en: Two volumes offset by half a storey: a one-storey wing beside a one-and-a-half-storey wing, with the garage tucked under the bedrooms and pushed forward, and a recessed entrance under the eaves. Salmon, buff or brown stone with wood or metal infill panels; both roofs share one low-pitched material. The interior stair does the work the façade shows.
origin_en: A plan type more than a style, dominant across North American suburbs from the mid-1950s: two volumes offset by half a storey, the garage under the bedrooms and pushed forward, a recessed entrance under the eaves. blurb_en: Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie idiom, filtered through 1960s Montreal: relentless horizontality, low pyramidal or multi-hipped roofs with deep soffits, upper windows tucked right under the eaves and running around the corners as ribbons, long “Roman” brick or long-cut stone, and one-storey wings (garage, porch, solarium) that stretch the composition sideways. Asymmetrical, and the most architect-driven of the phase-3 types.
origin_en: Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie idiom of 1900–1915, revived and simplified in the 1950s–60s Contemporary house: relentless horizontality, low pyramidal or multi-hipped roofs with deep soffits, upper windows tucked under the eaves and wrapping the corners as ribbons, long "Roman" brick or long-cut stone, one-storey wings that stretch the composition sideways. Asymmetrical and the most architect-driven of the Phase 3 types; the by-law's insistence on the Roman brick module is the tell.
