style_label: Boomtown (false front) / Vernaculaire industriel (Québec industrial vernacular)
siting_landscape: Exclusive to the aire de paysage Côte-Saint-Paul, where it is common; examples elsewhere in the borough are rare. It is not the principal type of any single landscape unit. | Generally contiguous, front setback 1.5 to 4 m, and where a series occurs the façades form regular alignments. | But there are detached examples set at the back of the lot, with a deep front yard in front of them — variante 1, and a relatively frequent one. | The front yard is usually barely landscaped.

articulation: The façade composition is often very simple: door in the centre, one window each side, with an awning, galerie or porch of varying size added. | The top of the building is usually finished with a metal flashing; more complex crownings are made with a worked sheet-metal cornice, with amortissements — small piers at each end of the roof — or with a parapet at the centre. | More decorated examples carry stone insertions on the façade: low reliefs in geometric patterns, or stone window surrounds.

blurb_en: One storey, flat roof, a door between two windows, and a flashing or a worked metal cornice for a crown. Three hundred and fifty-two of them, all but a handful inside one landscape area, Côte-Saint-Paul — and, tellingly, not the principal type of a single landscape unit anywhere. It is the cheap detached house of the borough's last frontier, built while the plex was filling everything closer in.
origin_en: Boomtown is the most widely distributed form on this site, and the Sud-Ouest is one of the places that extend its range. What is unusual here is the count and the confinement: the study puts a number on it — 352 — and puts it in one corner of one borough. Compare the Rosemont shoebox, a one-storey flat-roofed self-built house of the same decades that another Montréal borough treats as a protected type of its own.

siting_landscape: Contiguous, and in most cases with no front setback at all — which is exactly why the stair to the second dwelling is inside the building. | The façades form regular alignments. | Present in every sector lotted at the end of the industrialisation period, 1825–1875.
massing: Rectangular plan with no projections, two storeys, flat roof. | The ground floor is barely raised — two or three risers. | A small balcony over the entrance doors is possible, mainly where the doors are paired.
articulation: Two modes of composition, and they are what tells the variants apart: doors separated, or doors paired. | With separated doors, doors and windows alternate along the ground floor and the ground-floor openings frequently fail to line up with those above. | With paired doors there are two vertical alignments, one of them holding the two doors with a balcony over them. | The socle is one or two courses of rusticated stone; on altered buildings the stone is often replaced by exposed concrete. | The crowning is a moulded cornice, more or less worked according to the case.
openings: Originally sash or casement with or without a transom; most of what survives is replacement, frequently sliders. | The dominant proportion is one width to half a height, and segmental-arched openings are frequent. | Doors plain, with or without a transom, the transom's height variable.

blurb_en: The first multi-family building type built in the borough, and the one the exterior stair eventually killed. Two dwellings stacked under a flat roof, hard on the street line, both front doors at ground level and the upper dwelling reached by a stair inside. It loses ground after 1880 and is finally displaced by the triplex with exterior stair around 1900 — which is the whole argument of this borough in one sentence.
origin_en: The plex before the stair went outside. Reading this record against the triplex with exterior stair (2.6) gives the mechanism directly: no setback, so no room for a stair in the yard, so the stair eats interior floor area instead.

blurb_en: Two dwellings over three occupied levels under a false mansard — the type that answers the question of what Montréal built before the exterior stair, and the one the study reaches for when it explains why the fabric of the 1875–1945 period is not homogeneous. Built with no setback in the earlier phase and with one in the later, which is when the projecting window and the raised ground floor arrive.
origin_en: It is the plex family's tallest pre-1900 member and its closest relative to the Second Empire terraces of Ville-Marie and the Plateau. The study notes a rare third dwelling squeezed in — variante 2, a triplex with a false-mansard roof — which is how the boundary between duplex and triplex actually behaves on the ground.

Two storeys over a ground floor raised five to ten risers, a false mansard across the front, an oriel often enough, rusticated stone at the base and brick or cut stone above. In the Sud-Ouest it is the exception rather than the rule: the study introduces it by saying the borough is otherwise made of modest, often high-density residential buildings.

Two storeys, four or six dwellings, and a single central interior stair reaching all of them — « Cet immeuble à logements se différencie du plex par la présence d’un escalier commun intérieur pour accéder aux logements ». Ce bâtiment possède un hall d’entrée commun qui dessert de six à douze logements. »

siting_landscape: Contiguous, with a front margin of 2 to 4.5 m; the front façades generally form regular alignments. | Front yards stay sober, sometimes with a low metal fence between yard and public realm. | Built at the same time as the triplex with exterior stair, from 1900 to 1945, in the sectors that needed less density — furthest from downtown. Commonest in the aire de paysage Côte-Saint-Paul.
massing: A simple rectangular plan, two storeys, flat roof. | The ground floor is raised two to four risers above grade. | A balcony at the upper level, and under it a covered entrance porch at ground level. | An exterior stair reaches the upper dwelling; it is generally L-shaped, since the front margin is not deep enough for a straight run.

blurb_en: The triplex's smaller twin, built simultaneously and for the same reason, in the parts of the borough that did not need three dwellings on a lot. Two storeys, flat roof, a setback of two to four and a half metres, and an L-shaped stair climbing that setback because it is not deep enough for a straight one — a detail the study records and which explains the curved and dog-legged stairs of Montréal better than any folklore about snow.
origin_en: The study is explicit that this type and the triplex with exterior stair (2.6) are the same event: « Le duplex avec escalier extérieur a été construit de façon simultanée au triplex avec escalier extérieur, soit à partir de 1900 jusqu’à 1945 ». Density, not date, is what separates them.

blurb_en: The top of the plex family: three storeys, two dwellings per floor, and — the detail that matters — one shared access for the two dwellings on the top floor. origin_en: This is where the plex family ends and the apartment building begins. The multiplex still gives most dwellings their own front door but concedes a shared one at the top; the maison d'appartements (3.1) concedes the whole stair; the immeuble d'appartements (3.3) concedes a common hall serving six to twelve. Read the four records in order and the boundary the canonical layer draws between plex-family and apartment-house-common-hall is the study's own.

siting_landscape: The commonest variant of the triplex in the borough, and the base type of the urban fabric of four-built-sided blocks with an « H » ruelle that is so typical of several Montréal quarters. | Contiguous, front margin between 2.5 and 5 m. The alignment of façades is not regular. | The front yard is often characterised by a low metal fence. | Principal type in eleven of the sixty-five landscape units. Only the two interior-stair plexes it displaced are named principal in more of them — the duplex with interior stair in thirteen, the triplex with interior stair in twelve — which is what a type that arrives in 1900 looks like measured against types with a fifty-year head start.
massing: A rectangular body, sometimes with projecting windows on every level. | Generally a rear extension, whose position is reversed from one building to the next so as to make shared yards. | Flat roof, three storeys, ground floor raised two to three risers. | An exterior access stair climbs to the first floor. Balconies are possible.
articulation: Two principal modes of composition. The first is asymmetrical on two vertical bays: the first aligns the exterior stair, the first-floor entrance doors and a window and balcony at the second; the second is windows only and may project from the plane of the wall. In this mode the ground-floor dwelling's door is frequently set apart from both alignments — at the centre of the façade, or just behind the stair. | The second is symmetrical on three vertical bays: a central bay of doors and balconies, flanking bays of windows. At the first floor the two doors to the upper dwellings can sit at the centre, and the exterior stair is then slightly curved; or the stair runs straight to doors placed in one of the side bays. | The first-floor entrance porch is frequently recessed behind the plane of the façade. | The socle is one or two courses of rusticated stone. | The crowning stands out as a moulded wood cornice, a stone cornice, or a pedimented parapet.
openings: Mainly sash or casement, with or without a transom. Proportion generally one width to half a height, though windows may be paired into a nearly square opening. | Doors plain and with a transom; at the first floor the two doors to the upper dwellings are sometimes paired. | Lintels expressed as a cut-stone band or as soldier-course brick, straight or in a segmental arch.
materials: Rusticated stone at the socle. | Brick the dominant cladding, though some buildings are clad in rusticated stone. | Balconies and stair treads in wood; guards in metal.
blurb_en: The archetypal Montréal house, and this is the document that says how it happened. It appears from 1900. Its parent is the block with an « H » ruelle and four built sides. Its defining feature is not the stair as an object but the stair as a consequence: the front-setback requirement gave the stair somewhere to go, and putting it there kept the interior floor area and saved heating a shared hall. Eleven of the borough's sixty-five landscape units name it as their principal type.
origin_en: The mechanism, verbatim from the study's synthèse: « l’obligation de l’implantation avec une marge de recul avant amènera la translation de l’escalier d’accès aux logements des étages supérieurs vers l’extérieur, ce qui donnera la caractéristique si typique des bâtiments des quartiers montréalais de cette époque ». The sequence is dated: lotting without a ruelle and building with no setback « ne sera abandonnée que vers la fin des années 1880 »; this type « fait son apparition principalement à partir de 1900 »; the duplex with exterior stair and the multiplex follow shortly after.

Side margins vary where they are paired; the front setback is generously large, 5 to 8 m. | Front yards regularly carry real landscaping — hedges or trees — and a parking space. | The result, the study says, is generally a break with traditional urban development; the sets are homogeneous by street segment or by block, according to how each project was planned.

blurb_en: The redevelopment house: two storeys under a pitched roof, an integral garage, a deep planted setback, built from the 1960s and mostly from the 1980s in the cleared parts of La Petite-Bourgogne and in the sectors reached by the Opération 20 000 logements. The study is blunt about what it is — « généralement en rupture avec les développements urbains traditionnels » — and equally clear that each project is internally consistent.
origin_en: No canonical form is claimed for this record. It is the one Sud-Ouest residential type that does not match anything else on this site: not the 19th-century terrace the English word town house normally names, not the plex it replaced, and not a suburban model catalogue. It belongs to the fifth phase and to the machinery of urban renewal, and it is recorded here because the borough's own typology records it.

One storey. | Pitched two-slope, pavilion or hipped roof; the ridge is sometimes parallel to the street and sometimes at right angles to it. Where the pitch is steeper the attic is occupied. | The ground floor is raised two to five risers above grade.

What the Sud-Ouest fiche adds is the ordinary end of the story: not a prize-winning NHA neighbourhood but a few streets in Côte-Saint-Paul where the standard plan was dropped into an existing grid.

name_en: Stone house in the French tradition
name_fr: La maison de tradition française en pierre
source_ref: RPCQ, Site patrimonial du Vieux-Terrebonne (id 231571), MCC 2026
source_generation: site-level éléments caractéristiques + named classed examples
siting_landscape: Sited on the edge of a narrow street in the heart of the Vieux-Terrebonne, detached.
massing: Rectangular ground plan; the carré low and barely raised above the ground. | One and a half storeys. | Steep two-slope roof with short larmiers and no dormers. | Chimney stack and perron are the only projections the fiche records.
articulation: Cut-stone chimney stacks set staggered ("en chicane") in the gable walls. | Wooden window casings, an S-shaped wall anchor (esse), a wooden balustrade.
openings: Rectangular casement windows with small panes. | Main door of wood, panelled, with a transom.
materials: Roughcast stone masonry over a stone foundation. | Cedar-shingle roof covering.
blurb_en: One building carries this type, and it is a reconstruction around old walls. The maison Bélisle of about 1759 at 844 rue Saint-François-Xavier is a low roughcast-stone carré of one and a half storeys, barely raised off the ground, under a steep two-slope roof with short larmiers, no dormers and cedar shingle, with casement windows of small panes and cut-stone chimney stacks staggered in the gable walls. The RPCQ calls what remains of it "un rare témoin du noyau villageois du milieu du XVIIIe siècle".
origin_en: Jacques Perras (1725–1786), écrivain du munitionnaire du Roy, took a land concession in 1759 and had the house built shortly afterwards, when Lepage's bourg was some four decades old; by 1781 the village counted more than sixty dwellings. The RPCQ reads the house as an example of "la maison rurale québécoise d'inspiration française" — the French model progressively adapted by local know-how to the climate and the available materials. It was considerably altered between 1830 and 1850, when coyaux were added at the ends of the rafters and the roof took on the flared larmiers it now shows, and an angled corner door was cut at the turn of the twentieth century. The Bélisle family bought it in 1916 and held it for much of the century. It escaped the 1922 fire that destroyed most of the houses between rues Sainte-Marie and Chapleau south of rue Saint-Pierre, but it burned in 1999 — only the masonry could be kept, and the building was restored in 2002–2003 to return it to its eighteenth-century appearance. What stands today is therefore old walls with new everything else, and the record should be read that way. It is classed as an immeuble patrimonial (30 October 1973) with an aire de protection of the same date, and the protection covers the exterior and the interior but not the land.

blurb_en: The merchants' house of the crest — stone or brick, sometimes wood, under a tin roof, standing well back from rue Saint-Louis in a fenced and planted front yard with its old outbuildings beside it, and ornamented, the declaration says, elaborately. It is the only one of the four types here whose record rests on the sector paragraph alone, with no classed building behind it, which is why its styles are provisional and its massing and openings rows are empty.
origin_en: A migration, and a datable one. The RPCQ's fiche for the maison Roussil explains that the building of the second manor at the site of today's parc Masson at the end of the eighteenth century "entraîne une migration de la bourgeoisie vers la rue Saint-Louis. Plusieurs résidences cossues en pierre ou en bois sont alors érigées le long de cette artère." The fur merchants McTavish attracted after 1802 began it; the francophone business élite that followed Joseph Masson's purchase of the seigneury in 1832 continued it; and the street kept filling through the nineteenth century, which is why the surviving houses on it run from the maison Joseph-Augé of 1798–1801 through the maison Roussil of about 1830 to the maison Hercule-Masson of about 1880–1900, the maison Louis-de-Gonzague-Masson of about 1896 and the maison Raymond-Masson of about 1910–1935. Rue Saint-Louis carries 44 of the site's 225 associated RPCQ records, more than any other street.

Photograph © Jeangagnon, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:930,_rue_Saint-Louis,_Terrebonne.jpg Address match: 930 rue Saint-Louis is one of the 225 RPCQ records associated with the declared site. phase_title: The Masson seigneury and the bourgeois crest
source_ref: RPCQ, Site patrimonial du Vieux-Terrebonne (id 231571), MCC 2026

siting_landscape: Set on the edge of rue Saint-Louis, in the bourgeois sector of the Vieux-Terrebonne.
massing: Rectangular ground plan, two and a half storeys, detached. | Two-slope roof of medium pitch with slightly flared larmiers. | Chimney and gallery are the projections the fiche records.
articulation: Symmetry of the principal façade and regular ordering of the openings. | Carved window casings (chambranles sculptés). | Quoins (chaînages d'angle). | Cornice underlined with modillons; corbels; a wooden balustrade. | Wide two-headed cut-stone chimney stacks joined by a low wall at each end of the roof.

blurb_en: The maison Roussil of about 1830 on rue Saint-Louis, classed in 1972 and given an aire de protection in 1975, is the anchor — a rectangular stone house of two and a half storeys under two slightly flared slopes, its front elevation laid in rubble dressed to look like cut stone, symmetrical and regularly fenestrated, with carved chambranles, quoins, a cornice on modillons, and wide two-headed cut-stone chimney stacks joined by a low wall at each end of the roof.
origin_en: Built by and for Noël-Théodore Roussil (c. 1798–1890), master joiner and militia captain, as both dwelling and craftsman's workshop — a door cut in the west elevation once gave onto the shop. The RPCQ reads the house as representative of the influence of neoclassicism on Québec residential architecture in the nineteenth century, expressed in the symmetry of the main façade, the regular ordering of the openings, the medium-pitched roof and the ornamental vocabulary of carved casings, quoins and modillon cornice; Roussil gave every interior bay a different treatment, which the fiche says is what gives the house its originality. As master joiner he is said to have taken contracts for work on the parish church and on the seigneurial office; as militia captain he sided with the loyalists in the rebellions of 1837–1838, and some authors hold that patriotes were held in the house awaiting transfer to the prison du Pied-du-Courant in Montréal. A second example stands a few doors away — the maison Alexandre et Joseph Roussil, built in stone about 1830 by Noël-Théodore's uncles "tout près de celle de leur neveu", two and a half storeys under a tôle à baguettes roof, cited by the Ville on 13 September 2021.

name_en: Small-gabarit vernacular village house of the Bas-de-la-Côte
name_fr: La maison vernaculaire villageoise du Bas-de-la-Côte
source_ref: RPCQ, Site patrimonial du Vieux-Terrebonne (id 231571), MCC 2026
source_generation: site-level éléments caractéristiques + named classed examples
siting_landscape: Set on relatively straight, narrow public streets forming an orthogonal grid. | Minimal front setbacks, producing "un fort encadrement urbain" — a hard, continuous street wall. | Plain and limited front-yard treatment; no ornamental planting is claimed by the source. | The ground falls away from rue Saint-Louis down towards the river, so the street wall steps down the slope. | The ruelle du Passant links rues Sainte-Marie and Saint-André through the block.
massing: Small in gabarit in both height and width — the declaration's only dimensional statement about them. | Wood galleries and balconies of traditional make project over the street.
articulation: Buildings set at street intersections carry distinguishing architectural detail, notably angled corner doors.
materials: Wood cladding or brick masonry. | Tin roofing.
blurb_en: The ordinary house of the Bas-de-la-Côte, and by count the commonest thing in the declared site — small in height and width, wood or brick under a tin roof, set almost on the street line so that the row of them makes a continuous urban wall, with wooden galleries and balconies over the footway and an angled door where a house turns a corner. The declaration names no storey count, roof form or window type for it, so neither does this record.
origin_en: The bourg's fabric rather than any one architect's product. Louis Lepage de Sainte-Claire began conceding urban lots from 1720, and by 1781 the village counted more than sixty dwellings; the grid of narrow streets dropping from rue Saint-Louis to the rivière des Mille-Îles was laid out before 1850 and filled with modest houses for the artisans, tradespeople and workers who served the mills and, later, the grain and fur trades. The RPCQ's valeur architecturale calls the result "un ensemble de résidences villageoises de petit gabarit et d'architecture vernaculaire". A fire ravaged part of Terrebonne in 1922, destroying most of the houses between rues Sainte-Marie and Chapleau south of rue Saint-Pierre, so what stands in that stretch is in part post-1922 rebuilding on the old lot pattern.

phase_title: The French-regime bourg
name_fr: La maison d'esprit français (courant colonial français)
source_ref: Ville de Trois-Rivières, Répertoire des courants architecturaux (Patri-Arch); RPCQ id 93531 (MCC); MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Trois-Rivières, 2014
source_generation: city-wide courant fiche, cross-read against the declared-site texts
roofing: cedar shingle; traditional tin in town
siting_landscape: Built at ground level, without a cellar, on shallow stone footings; the house is entered from the flat. | In town, set with the façade directly on the street, so that the party walls carried above the roof do the work a setback would otherwise do. | Stone was almost absent from the Trois-Rivières district and had to be brought from the south shore, so the rare stone houses belonged to the well-off or the notable; stone was otherwise reserved for mills, convents and churches.
massing: Rectangular body close to the ground, squat in proportion. | A single ground floor under an inhabited attic. | Steep straight two-slope roof, pitches reaching as much as 55 degrees; some roofs hipped on four slopes. | Short straight eaves (larmiers), or later slightly upturned ones. | Some rural houses longer and shallower, like the manoir Boucher-De Niverville; others squarer and more massive.
articulation: Few ornaments beyond the chambranles framing the openings; simplicity and bareness are the point. | Massive stone chimney stacks, sometimes set "en chicane" — not all on the same roof slope. | Fire-break party walls carried above the roof in urban settings. | Where a house was later brought up to date, the neoclassical additions read as additions — at the maison Georges-De Gannes a pedimented entrance portal, a cornice, cornice returns and carved window surrounds.
openings: Asymmetrical façade composition; openings distributed by need rather than by rule. | Openings few in number, to limit heat loss, and doubled by storm doors and storm windows. | Double casement windows with small panes, working shutters. | Few or no dormers, and where present, gabled and small; dormers appear only at the end of the French regime, as a new way of inhabiting the attic.
materials: Squat carré of rubble stone or of massive squared timber, sometimes rendered in roughcast or covered with vertical boards; a slight batter in the walls. | Roof traditionally of cedar shingle; in town the wooden shingle often gives way to traditional tin.
conservation: Prefer: preserve the imposing volume and the squat aspect of these houses, and the asymmetrical distribution of the openings, which should also stay few in number. | Prefer: use traditional materials — stone and wood for the walls, wood shingle or traditional tin for the roofs, and wood for doors and windows. Avoid modern materials such as vinyl and aluminium. | Avoid: adding ornament. Simplicity and bareness are what characterise these buildings. | Avoid: moving, enlarging, adding or altering doors, windows and dormers. | Avoid: uprooting old buildings from the place they were built. The City's own fiche makes the point about the 1781 windmill, moved to the university grounds in 1974: the move saved it from demolition but cost it part of its historical meaning.
blurb_en: The house the first colonists built and the notables rebuilt in stone: a squat rectangle sitting straight on the ground without a cellar, one floor under a steep roof that could reach 55 degrees, few windows because the winter demanded few, and massive chimneys because it demanded many. In town the party walls run up past the roof as fire-breaks. Trois-Rivières had almost no local stone, so the stone version was always the exception — the mark of a family with the means to ship it from the south shore.
origin_en: Brought from rural north-western France — Brittany, Normandy, the Île-de-France — and adapted fast to a country with different materials and a harsher winter. The RPCQ says of the declared site that "le Régime français a légué… la maison Saint-François… des résidences de notables en pierre, comme le manoir de Tonnancour (1795-1797)". The form outlived the Conquest by the isolation of the population, and buildings put up between 1780 and 1820 still show it; from the 1820s, crossed with English neoclassicism, it produced the maison de tradition québécoise. The 1908 fire destroyed several of the city's French-regime buildings, including the parish church and the maison des Gouverneurs.
photo_credit: Maison Georges-De Gannes, 834 rue des Ursulines, in the site patrimonial de Trois-Rivières (October 2020) — built about 1756, classed as an immeuble patrimonial in 1961. © Cantons-de-l'Est, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 — https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Trois-Rivieres,_Quebec_-_834_rue_des_Ursulines.jpg

phase_title: Forestry capital of the Mauricie
name_en: Well-to-do bourgeois house in stone and brick (maison cossue)
name_fr: La demeure bourgeoise / la résidence cossue
source_ref: Ville de Trois-Rivières, Répertoire des courants architecturaux (Patri-Arch); RPCQ id 93531 (MCC); MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Trois-Rivières, 2014
source_generation: declared-site texts (RPCQ + Plan de conservation) read with the City's Néoclassicisme fiche
style_label: Québec neoclassical / Second Empire / mansard / Victorian eclecticism
roofing: traditional tin; copper on the grandest
siting_landscape: Along the terrasse Turcotte and rue des Ursulines, where the declared site's occupation is at its thinnest — the RPCQ contrasts "la faible densité d'occupation en bordure de la rue des Ursulines et de la terrasse Turcotte" with the smaller, more densely built lots of rues Saint-Pierre, Saint-François-Xavier, Saint-Louis and des Casernes. | Deeper front margins than in the institutional blocks, and a marked tree cover, in the Plan de conservation's unité de paysage of "maisons urbaines individuelles". | The grandest georgian houses stand alone in the middle of a large lot.
massing: Rectangular body well clear of the ground, two or two and a half storeys. | Two- or four-slope roof of medium or shallow pitch; mansard roofs on the Second Empire examples. | Monumental in effect rather than in size; the Plan de conservation calls the group homogeneous in volume, height and material. | Few or no projecting elements such as balconies and galleries in the neoclassical register; on the Second Empire and eclectic examples, a projecting central bay marking the entrance, turrets, and polygonal projections.
articulation: Order, symmetry and sobriety are the three watchwords of the neoclassical register — regularity in the plan as much as in the distribution of the openings, sometimes to the point of austerity. | Classical ornament drawn from antiquity — pediment, round arch over the openings, columns, piers, pilasters, quoins, cornice returns. | On the eclectic examples, an elaborate crown — cornices on consoles and modillions, carved lintels, worked cornices, dormers under semicircular pediments. | Main entrance marked by a porch or a portal.
openings: Casement or sash windows, with panes. | Round-arched doors and windows and oculi in the palladian register; segmental-arched openings on the later ones. | Symmetrical arrangement of openings and chimneys, the English signature on a house otherwise French in its siting and roof.
materials: Smooth wall surfaces — cut stone, roughcast, brick or wood boards. | Stone in the earlier houses; the Plan de conservation records that the declared site's ten stone buildings include the classed houses, and that only two stone dwellings postdate 1900. | Brick predominates in the turn-of-the-century group, which the Plan de conservation describes as "résidences individuelles en brique à deux niveaux d'habitation". | Copper roofing on at least one — the house of about 1850 at 858 terrasse Turcotte.
conservation: Avoid: cladding and roofing materials on the house and its dormers, and railing patterns, that do not answer to the noble character of this architecture. | Avoid: the combination that has stripped one such house of all its attributes — replacement cladding, replacement window and door models, and unsuitable railings, applied together while the overall composition was respected.
blurb_en: The merchant's house of a river town that had money before it had industry, standing back from the street behind mature trees on the thinnest-built edge of the old core. Stone in the first half of the nineteenth century, brick by the turn of the twentieth, always well clear of the ground and always symmetrical — the neoclassical order held on here longer than anywhere else in Québec, and when it finally loosened it did so into Second Empire mansards and eclectic crowns rather than into anything plainer.
origin_en: English neoclassicism arrived with the British and Scottish military engineers and architects at the start of the nineteenth century, and the City's fiche notes that in Trois-Rivières it gave ground to eclecticism more slowly than elsewhere, even reviving early in the twentieth century as Beaux-Arts. Its bourgeois version is what the RPCQ means by "des maisons cossues", the first of the two residential registers it says characterise the declared site — the other being "des immeubles d'habitation construits sur des lots étroits". The same opulent-house form is described under `maison-cossue-ornamented` at Vieux-Terrebonne, where the declaration reads it off the rue Saint-Louis crest; here it is read off the terrasse Turcotte and rue des Ursulines.

phase_title: The fire and the reconstruction
name_en: The 1908 reconstruction block — brick, flat-roofed, built all at once
name_fr: Le bâti de la reconstruction d'après l'incendie de 1908
source_ref: Ville de Trois-Rivières, Répertoire des courants architecturaux (Patri-Arch); RPCQ id 93531 (MCC); MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Trois-Rivières, 2014
source_generation: assembled from the reconstruction passages of the four sources; no single fiche describes it
style_label: Victorian eclecticism / Second Empire / mansard / Boomtown (false front)
siting_landscape: The rebuilt quarter occupies the ground between the river and rues Bonaventure, Champlain and Saint-Georges, where the fire of 22 June 1908 stopped. | Streets were widened and in places redrawn as part of the reconstruction; inside the declared site the widths of rues des Casernes and des Ursulines and the public space on the site of the destroyed parish church are listed by the RPCQ as characteristic elements produced by the post-fire works. | The RPCQ notes that in the south-west of the declared site "quelques rues plus larges témoignent du réaménagement qui a suivi le grand incendie de 1908"; the former couvent des Filles de Jésus is set back from the roadway for the same reason. | Continuous street frontage, the buildings taking the full width of their lots.
massing: Two to three storeys, occasionally four, under a flat roof. | Rows built as rows, by a small number of hands, within four years — the source of the quarter's evenness. | Inside the declared site, 13 buildings — close to 30 % of it — went up between 1908 and 1925, among them the three-storey Appartements Laviolette of 1918, put up in place of a building the flames had probably taken.
articulation: Parapets and cornices on consoles; keystones, sills and lintels at the openings; brick patterning and banding. | The Plan de conservation lists exactly these as the marks of the brick urban houses and immeubles à logements built at the turn of the twentieth century in the declared site. | Some of the rebuilt houses are Second Empire — the City's fiche captions the imposing house at 186-190 rue Bonaventure, with its turret, carved lintels and worked cornice, as built after the great fire of 1908. | The City's Maison à mansarde fiche makes the same point for the modest register, noting mansard houses built after the 1908 fire alongside the 1870-1900 majority.
openings: Symmetrical arrangement of openings, wood doors usually at the centre of the façade, many with a glazed transom. | Casement windows with panes and sash windows are the two commonest types, with moulded wood chambranles and sometimes shutters or louvred blinds. | Bay windows at ground level on some turn-of-the-century houses; oriels on several of the immeubles à logements.
materials: Brick, decisively. Of the 45 buildings in the declared site, 28 are brick-clad and 18 of those postdate 1908. | Across the city the shift is measurable — a built stock still mostly of wood at the start of the twentieth century was 55 % brick-housed by 1931, in part through the post-fire construction.
blurb_en: A quarter rebuilt in four years by, as the City puts it, a handful of architects and contractors — and the evenness that produced is the heritage claim, not a side effect of it. Brick, flat roofs, two to four storeys in continuous rows, ornament gathered into parapets, cornices on consoles, keystones, lintels and brick banding. The fire took the commercial centre and largely spared the old core, so this fabric surrounds the declared site rather than filling it; but the site's widened streets, its public space on the burnt parish church's ground, and thirteen of its forty-five buildings belong to the same four years.
origin_en: The fire of 22 June 1908 began in a hay store, pushed back the city's eight firefighters within a quarter of an hour, and brought help from Shawinigan, Grand-Mère, Québec and Montréal. How much it destroyed is genuinely contested and the figures are set out with their attributions in the notes on the place page — the City says "près de 800 bâtiments", its own Patri-Arch study says "environ 200 bâtiments", Radio-Canada says a quarter of the city and no casualties, and the UQTR account reconciles the two counts as buildings-including-sheds against residences. What is not contested is the speed and the singleness of the rebuilding, and its material — a city still largely of wood in 1900 was 55 % brick-housed by 1931.

phase_title: Pulp and paper — the workers' parishes
source_ref: Ville de Trois-Rivières, Répertoire des courants architecturaux (Patri-Arch); RPCQ id 93531 (MCC); MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Trois-Rivières, 2014
source_generation: city-wide courant fiche (web summary + fiche complète), cross-read against the declared-site texts
style_label: Boomtown (false front) / Vernaculaire industriel (Québec industrial vernacular)
roofing: low-slope tin, then tar-and-membrane flat roof
siting_landscape: Little raised above the ground. | Found in numbers in the village cores and also isolated in the countryside; in the city, spread through the quartiers Saint-Philippe, Sainte-Cécile and Notre-Dame in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and through the oldest quarters of Cap-de-la-Madeleine. | Developers often chose party-wall, semi-detached or three-storey models to make more of urban land whose cost kept rising. | Inside the declared site, the Plan de conservation finds "des maisons ouvrières en brique à deux niveaux de type boomtown ornées sobrement" among the buildings raised from the end of the nineteenth century in the îlots résidentiels.
massing: Cubic or rectangular volume, generally of two storeys. | Flat roof, or of low pitch falling to the rear. | The plan is generally modest and may be larger or smaller; two contiguous dwellings are not uncommon. | Few projections apart from a gallery under an awning, or a balcony at the upper floor. | The projections are often a large gallery running the whole width of the main façade, with a balcony above on the central third of the independent awning that shelters it; cast-iron railings — the "fers de galerie" popular in the second half of the nineteenth century — are frequent.
articulation: Ornament concentrated in the upper part of the façade, by way of a cornice, a parapet or brick patterning. | Other, discreet ornament — chambranles, corner boards, brick flat arches. | Because the roof becomes invisible, its presence is replaced by ornamental work in the form of a cornice or a parapet — the raised front that gives the form its name. | Some parapets end in steps on the side elevations, following the roof's fall to the rear; some carry amortissements; some carry fine curved cornices or cornices on paired consoles. | Some examples are sober and stripped; others take the eclectic decoration of the Victorian period comfortably, and a few carry the rare curb of a false Second Empire mansard.
openings: Regular, symmetrical distribution of openings. | Casement windows with large panes, and possibly small attic-space windows. | The windows are of vertical proportion throughout and may carry louvred shutters. | A great variety of small windows for ventilating the attic space, pierced in the high clear front of these houses, gives them a definite interest — and in Trois-Rivières they take diamond and other particular shapes that the City's own inventory calls a local peculiarity, little found elsewhere in Québec.
materials: Cladding of wood clapboard or of brick — "parfois revêtue de bois, souvent bâtie en brique". | Later industrialisation of processes brought tar paper, slate-surfaced bituminous felt (papier-brique) and asbestos-cement shingle, available in several shapes. | Inside the declared site the boomtown examples are brick.
conservation: Avoid: adding annexes to the body of the building, which cramps the simple cubic volume of the Boomtown house. Exaggerated raising of the modest volume when a basement is dug, and changing the roof profile by adding prefabricated trusses, are two further transformations that greatly damage its integrity. | Prefer: replace windows within their original bays, to the original model, without changing their dimensions and above all without widening them, keeping any transom in the upper third. | Prefer: keep the attic-ventilation openings. Do not block them up and fit derisory little louvred vents in their place, and above all do not remove them. False shutters are to be banned. | Prefer: where a house has suffered a proliferation of materials applied over repeated interventions, use the next renovation to give it back an exemplary simplicity. | Prefer: since tar paper and asbestos-cement shingle are no longer on the market, repairs may be made to the more visible parts using material taken from the less visible ones; otherwise, replace with light claddings such as wood or fibre-cement. | Avoid: roughcast render (stucco or acrylic), which masks every traditional element of a building.
blurb_en: Two storeys, a flat roof or one falling gently to the rear, and a front wall carried up past it into a cornice or a parapet so the building looks taller from the street than it is from the lane. Balloon-framed, so it went up fast; clapboard or brick; a big gallery across the front under an independent awning, with a balcony on its middle third and cast-iron railings. Trois-Rivières has enough of them, the City says, for the form to count as characteristic of the city — and the small diamond attic vents punched into the high clear front are a trifluvien signature the inventory says is little found elsewhere in Québec.
origin_en: The form is one of the strongest comparisons this site can make, because six independent municipalities describe it in their own words and the descriptions agree. Follow `boomtown-false-front` in the canonical layer to reach them — Québec City's thésaurus node tid 502, the flat-roofed types of the Ville de Gatineau's 2023 fiches, Saint-Lambert's two Boomtown fiches, the Ville de Lévis's styles-architecturaux fiche idfiche 10 ("1 à 2 étages… toiture plate ou à très faible pente vers l'arrière… parapet ou corniche, galerie couverte"), and this record. Every one of them arrives at the same building from a different municipal vocabulary. The mechanism is the same everywhere: balloon framing and sawn planks made construction fast and cheap after the crisis of 1870, and the boom towns of rapid industrial growth took it up for houses and shops alike. In Trois-Rivières it first coexisted with the maison villageoise de tradition québécoise and the mansard house, supplanted both at the turn of the twentieth century, and was in turn supplanted by the plex in the 1920s.

phase_title: Pulp and paper — the workers' parishes
name_en: Immeuble à logements — the plex of superposed flats
name_fr: L'immeuble à logements / l'immeuble de type « plex »
source_ref: Ville de Trois-Rivières, Répertoire des courants architecturaux (Patri-Arch); RPCQ id 93531 (MCC); MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Trois-Rivières, 2014
source_generation: city-wide courant fiche (web summary + fiche complète), cross-read against the declared-site texts
style_label: Vernaculaire industriel (Québec industrial vernacular) / Boomtown (false front)
siting_landscape: Built by property developers on cramped lots, as contiguous houses put up at speed to house the workers who supplied the labour for the city's rapid industrialisation. | Inside the declared site these are the îlots résidentiels — narrower parcels, more densely occupied, evidence of a stronger urban pressure during industrialisation than in the other sectors, though a tree cover survives in the back yards. | The RPCQ's second residential register for the declared site — "des immeubles d'habitation construits sur des lots étroits", against the maisons cossues.
massing: Cubic-looking volume, generally of two or three storeys. | Several dwellings, each with its own direct entrance from outside. | Numerous exterior extensions — balcony, gallery, stair. On the plainest examples these batteries of acrobatic stairs, balconies and galleries are the only decoration left. | Many have polygonal or rectangular projections; some have galleries and balconies carried on brick piers, sometimes arcaded; others have a setback cutting re-entrant angles wholly occupied by galleries and balconies in loggia, on masonry supports so strongly stated that they redraw the cubic volume. | Concrete foundations appear with this current.

materials: Traditional materials — brick cladding, wood openings. | Red or brown clay brick on many; concrete block imitating rusticated stone on others; limestone on a few exceptions. | Rare sheet-metal claddings imitating rusticated stone need upkeep or rust will make them disappear.
conservation: Prefer: where part of the brick cladding is redone, match the masonry colours carefully. Do not paint the brick or apply aluminium or vinyl cladding to it. When repointing, match the mortar to what is there, to avoid ugly demarcations. | Avoid: levelling off the stepped parapets. Consolidate them instead, by bracing them solidly on the roof side. | Avoid: altering the openings or blocking up the transoms. | Avoid: aluminium cladding on the wall crowns and the balcony shelters — it distorts them by swelling the volume out of all proportion. | Avoid: on contiguous or semi-detached houses, piecemeal renovation making changes for personal reasons at the expense of the aesthetic of the whole. | Prefer: today's required 42-inch (1.07 m) guard height can be reached by adding a second handrail to the existing 36-inch (0.914 m) railing, without spoiling what is there. Avoid guards of cut-out prefabricated boards and handrails of too slight a section.
blurb_en: When coal tar made the waterproof flat roof possible, the urban dwelling became a stack. Two or three storeys of superposed flats, each with its own door off the street reached by its own stair, put up at speed on cramped lots by the first property developers the city had seen, to house the mill workers. The oldest of them still carry the Boomtown's gallery-and-balcony arrangement — the fiche calls that their filiation — while the parapet turns from an applied cornice into stepped brick with friezes, and then into curves and counter-curves.
origin_en: The plex coexisted with the Boomtown house and then supplanted it about 1910; it is the house that matches the accelerated urban growth of 1910 to 1930, and by the 1920s the Patri-Arch Synthèse records it as the principal workers' dwelling in Trois-Rivières. The Depression and the Second World War left only an impoverished version, and it faded slowly in favour of the apartment block with a single common entrance. The interwar plex is a near relation of proto-rationalist architecture — the regular-framed, plainly detailed brick manufactories and warehouses of 1850-1890 — and it is the rational, simple, easily built and economical side of it that ties the plex to that current. The same superposed-dwelling form is followed through the canonical layer under `plex-superposed-units`.

Wood doors and windows are preferable to contemporary aluminium or PVC models. | Prefer: on the better-off examples, preserve or restore the chambranles, corner boards, turned columns and other ornament in their original material rather than replacing them with simplified modern elements. blurb_en: Two full storeys on a square plan under a shallow hipped roof — Frank Kidder's Four-square of 1891, sold through American plan catalogues on the strength of how much room it gave for the money, and taken up across Québec in the first half of the twentieth century. In Trois-Rivières it settled equally on the bare rural plains and in the denser village cores, and its ornament is a straightforward index of the first owner's means: chambranles only on one house, corner boards, turned columns and worked railings on the next.
origin_en: One branch of the industrial vernacular that standardised materials, mechanised the work and distributed plans through catalogues and magazines from the end of the nineteenth century, alongside the balloon frame that made building fast. The same square hipped block is followed through the canonical layer under `foursquare-hipped-2st`, where it can be set beside the versions catalogued by Saint-Lambert, Gatineau, Québec City and Lévis — a form that arrived from the United States by catalogue and was then renamed locally in every place it landed.

siting_landscape: First taken up by the anglophone elite, so unsurprisingly found among the residences of the directors of large companies — as at the place Freeman, formerly terrasse Saint-Maurice, which was reserved for the bosses of the Saint-Maurice Paper Company. Thereafter the architecture influenced every layer of society until the Second World War. | Where several stand together they can form ensembles whose forms marry to one another, avoiding the repetition of a single base model.
massing: Generally imposing volume on an articulated plan; the volume, however modest, is dynamically articulated. | Roofs of varied form with slopes of unequal length, and prominent chimneys. | Sheltered exterior spaces — perrons, galleries, terraces. | Coquettish little houses with roofs of unequal pitch, important chimneys and varied fenestration piercing walls of brick, stucco or cedar shingle.

openings: Numerous and diverse openings, with paired windows and dormers.
materials: Natural and traditional materials — stone, brick, stucco, cedar shingle, wood boards — sometimes combined with one another.
conservation: Prefer: since the Arts & Crafts spirit calls for a return to traditional materials and techniques, do not modernise these houses with contemporary industrial or synthetic materials. Wood doors and windows remain preferable to modern aluminium or PVC; the same advice applies to wall claddings. | Prefer: keep the expressed frame members, above all the rafters, under the wide roof overhangs. Do not box them into enamelled aluminium or vinyl on the pretext of ending repeated maintenance. Keep the wood shingle too, used in the railings of gallery-porches or as cladding. | Prefer: stucco cracks and repairs to it leave marks — patching stucco is next to impossible, so repairs must be concealed with a product prepared for external application on a cementitious material. | Avoid: since these houses are relatively recent, resist the temptation of a fake antiquity — false shutters bolted to the wall, removable false glazing bars fitted to make the glass look divided. blurb_en: Roofs of unequal slope running into one another, big chimneys, exposed rafters under wide overhangs, cedar shingle and stucco and stone used together, and windows put wherever the plan wanted them. The City's fiche declines to give a type description and says so: every case is unique and has its own characteristics. In Trois-Rivières it arrived with the paper company — place Freeman, the old terrasse Saint-Maurice, was the address of the Saint-Maurice Paper Company's bosses — and then filtered down through every layer of society until 1939.
origin_en: Ruskin and Morris, reacting against industrialisation and standardisation by way of English craft and the English country house; the movement converged with the garden city. Crossing to the United States it split into the Shingle Style of the east coast, the Prairie Style of the centre and the Craftsman of the west, and the catalogues and plan magazines carried all three across North America through the first half of the twentieth century. The City's fiche is candid that the idea did not survive the crossing — "en Amérique, le mouvement Arts & Crafts devient essentiellement un mouvement stylistique, sans portée sociale."

What replaced the farm is the only planned town on this site laid out on modernist principles rather than garden-city ones — building tall in order to free the ground, the shoreline made public, pedestrians separated from cars, and the blocks turned so the river shows between them. The cahier is unusually candid that this, and not the architecture, is what it is protecting: « Ce sont ces éléments urbains qui caractérisent ce secteur. » It also records that the plan's authority outlasted its authors — « une nouvelle ville sera planifiée selon des règles strictes dont l'influence est encore ressentie et dont l'esprit supporte les orientations actuelles » — which is why the Pointe-Nord de l'Île-des-Sœurs is one of the three territories Verdun's PIIA singles out for review of new construction. Set this beside the Westmount modern tower and the Outremont apartment blocks: same decade, same idiom, three different reasons for being there.

siting_landscape: Built to the street line inside the walled town, on the narrow lots of Dollier de Casson's 1672 tracé; the RPCQ's characteristic elements list the alignment of buildings on the public way, the high density of ground occupation and party-wall construction as the site's defining relation. | Interior courts and courettes in some sectors, reached from the street. | The surviving concentration is in sector 24.E.45, the quartier Bonsecours, which the cahier says is the one part of Vieux-Montréal that kept its residential vocation after 1850.
massing: Generally low — one or two storeys. | Two-slope or hipped roof of medium pitch. | Chimneys carried up in the plane of the gable walls, and firebreak walls between houses.
articulation: Not stated by either source beyond the masonry itself. The RPCQ describes this family in one sentence and does not treat its ornament.
openings: Wooden casement windows with small panes.
materials: Rubble masonry of roughly squared stone. | Grey limestone predominates in the site as a whole until 1850, after which a wide variety of stone types appears.
blurb_en: The oldest domestic form on this site and the one that recurs in six places: low walls of roughly squared rubble, a two-slope or hipped roof of medium pitch, chimneys rising in the plane of the gable walls, firebreak walls between neighbours, and small-paned wooden casements. In Vieux-Montréal it is an urban house — built to the street line, party-walled, on a narrow lot — rather than the freestanding rural house of the Île d'Orléans or the côtes.
origin_en: Ville-Marie was founded in 1642 as a missionary settlement and became the bridgehead of the fur trade. The Sulpicians became seigneurs of the island in 1663, and their superior François Dollier de Casson traced the first streets in 1672 with the notary-surveyor Bénigne Basset Des Lauriers: three streets parallel to the river and seven perpendicular to it. Between 1685 and 1800 the town was walled, and the wall fixed its form. The intendants' ordonnances then fixed the relation between street and building, including the alignment of construction; stone became the preferred material for new building, which is why so little of the wooden town survives. The form is the same one recorded on this site at Île d'Orléans, Charlesbourg, Québec, Terrebonne and Lachine — the same walls, the same roof, the same chimneys — with the difference that here it is packed against its neighbours.

phase_title: British regime — classical stone
name_en: Classical house of the British regime
name_fr: Édifice d’inspiration classique du Régime britannique
source_ref: RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005)
source_generation: RPCQ fiche 93528, sections « Valeur patrimoniale » and « Éléments caractéristiques » (fiche source: Ministère de la Culture et des Communications du Québec, 2004), read 17 August 2026; cross-read against the cahier's sector fiches 24.E.36, 24.E.39 and 24.E.43.
siting_landscape: Built on the public alignment, at high density, party-walled, like everything else inside the old town; the RPCQ lists the setting-back of certain administrative and public buildings as the exception that proves it. | The Plan des commissaires of 1804 gave the quarter a terrace along the river, an enlarged Champ-de-Mars and wider streets, and the three principal arteries bounding the site — rues de la Commune, Saint-Antoine and McGill — descend from it.
massing: Not stated. The RPCQ says only that the site's gauges are heterogeneous and very variable, particularly in height.
articulation: Symmetrical composition of the façade. | The classical orders recalled — Doric, Ionic, Corinthian. | Pediments and quoined angles.
openings: Not stated by either source for this family. | The RPCQ does record, as a characteristic of the site, the relation between lot and street "manifested by steps, carriage doors, railings, rights of way and several entrances — one on each façade giving on the street".
materials: Cut stone (pierre de taille). | Grey limestone predominant until 1850, then a wide variety of stone types.
blurb_en: What the British regime built when the walls came down: cut grey limestone, a symmetrical street front, an order recalled rather than reproduced, a pediment, quoined angles. The RPCQ treats it as the most numerous family in the site — « la forte proportion de bâtiments du Régime britannique d'inspiration classique » — and, because a site fiche describes a landscape rather than a house, it describes the family entirely in terms of the façade.
origin_en: From 1800 Montréal became the principal city of the two Canadas. The political upheavals of the 18th century, the Conquest and American independence among them, drove population growth and immigration, and dynamic import-export merchants replaced the magnates of the fur trade. The RPCQ's account of the change is architectural in one line: « Les maisons en bois des artisans font place aux résidences et édifices en pierre d'inspiration néoclassique. » The fortifications were demolished between 1801 and 1817 and three commissioners were appointed to plan the freed ground; their terrace along the river, enlarged Champ-de-Mars and wider streets are still the frame of the quarter. Grey limestone stayed the predominant material until 1850. The two great fires of 9 and 10 July 1852, which destroyed some 1 200 dwellings and left about 10 000 people homeless, ended wooden construction in the city outright and made stone the rule rather than the preference.

Shown as an example of the classical street front the RPCQ describes, not as a building either source attributes to this family by name.

phase_title: Warehouses, maisons-magasins and the faubourgs
name_en: Maison-magasin and warehouse with dwellings above
source_ref: RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005)
source_generation: RPCQ fiche 93528, section « Éléments caractéristiques » (fiche source: Ministère de la Culture et des Communications du Québec, 2004), read 17 August 2026; with the cahier's sector fiches 24.E.38, 24.E.40 and 24.E.42 and its historical chapter, printed pp. 34–35.
siting_landscape: Built to the street line in a continuous run, party-walled, on the blocks between rue de la Commune and rue Saint-Paul and along rues des Récollets, Sainte-Hélène, Saint-Pierre and Le Moyne. | Two-faced by design where the block runs through: the cahier records a relatively plain elevation on the goods-handling side and a far more elaborate one on the commercial side, on rue Saint-Paul.
massing: Flat roof. | Thick, projecting and often very ornamented cornice.
articulation: Heavy projecting cornice as the crowning element. | Ornament concentrated on the commercial elevation; showrooms for retail selling behind the ground-floor bays in the sector of the Bourses.
openings: Wide bays (« larges baies »).
materials: Mixed structure of timber, cast iron and stone. | Red brick. | Grey limestone on the older runs, in a site where grey limestone predominates until 1850 and a wide variety of stone types after it.
blurb_en: The building that made the port quarter and then, a century later, repopulated it. A mixed structure of timber, cast iron and stone; wide bays; a flat roof; a thick, projecting, often very ornamented cornice; red brick. In the runs between rue de la Commune and rue Saint-Paul it is frankly two-faced — sober where the goods came in, elaborate where they were sold. From the 1970s these are the buildings that were recycled into dwellings, which is how a quarter with a few hundred residents in the 1950s came to hold several thousand.
origin_en: Montréal became the undisputed metropolis of Canada in the second half of the 19th century, at the centre of a road, maritime and transcontinental rail network, and the old town turned into a financial and administrative city — the shop window of Canadian capitalism, in the RPCQ's phrase. Offices, banks, insurance head offices, warehouses and courthouses went up with great stylistic eclecticism. Then the fall: after 1945 Montréal lost the metropolitan role to Toronto, the economic centre moved north-west, and by the 1950s, the cahier records, retail had practically vanished from the old town and its residents numbered only a few hundred. Serious proposals for an expressway through Vieux-Montréal followed, and the protests against them led to the Québec government decreeing the quarter an arrondissement historique in 1964. Survival then meant new uses for empty floors, and the cahier states the mechanism plainly: « On y a recyclé plusieurs de ces bâtiments en condos, dont le premier exemple est celui des Cours Le Royer, posant ainsi le premier jalon d'un repeuplement du Vieux-Montréal. » The loft conversions of rue Saint-Paul and the faubourg des Récollets follow the same line.

phase_title: The Mille carré doré and the Victorian terrace
name_fr: Demeure bourgeoise isolée du Mille carré doré
source_ref: RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005)
source_generation: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005), sector fiches 24.E.29, 24.E.30, 24.E.28 and 24.E.3, and the historical chapter printed p. 30; with Héritage Montréal, Memento, « McGill and Golden Square Mile Houses », read 17 August 2026. The RPCQ fiche 93528 covers the declared site only and does not reach this quarter.
siting_landscape: Freestanding, often surrounded by gardens and outbuildings, on the south flank of the mountain. | The cahier values the sector as much for what the houses leave open as for the houses — « le dégagement qu'elle assure à la montagne ». | Only the part north of avenue du Docteur-Penfield falls inside the site patrimonial du Mont-Royal; sector 24.E.30, south of Sherbrooke, is explicitly outside it.
massing: Not stated for this sector. The neighbouring croissant Redpath, 24.E.28, is described as mostly three storeys under a two-slope roof — that is the cahier's figure for that sector, not for this one.
articulation: Not stated. The cahier calls the sector remarkable for « la qualité architecturale des bâtiments qui le composent » without describing that architecture.
openings: Not stated.
materials: Not stated for the sector. The cahier's neighbouring fiche 24.E.28 gives clay brick or stone for the Redpath crescent, and the site as a whole is characterised by grey limestone to 1850 and a wide variety of stone types after it.
blurb_en: The richest domestic architecture on the island of Montréal, and the least protected. A freestanding house of two and a half or three storeys standing in its own garden with its own outbuildings, on the slope between Sherbrooke and the mountain, built between about 1860 and 1935 in whichever revival was current — Italianate, Second Empire, Romanesque, Queen Anne, Beaux-Arts. The Ville grades the two sectors that hold them exceptionnelle. Neither carries an ensemble designation, and the columns below are empty because no document describes these houses as a type.
origin_en: The cahier's historical chapter puts it plainly: the north-west of the quartier Saint-Antoine, part of it running up the flank of the mountain, went on attracting the great Montréal bourgeoisie, which in the wake of the McTavishes and the McGills had sumptuous residences built by well-known architects — « On y compte les Allan, les Van Horne, les Forget » — and the sector would later be called the Square Mile. Héritage Montréal dates the golden age 1840–1930 and the buildings principally 1850–1930, and describes a commercial aristocracy that controlled two-thirds of the country's wealth. After the 1929 crash the families moved west to Westmount and the Town of Mount Royal, apartment and office buildings were put up in their gardens, and the quarter went, in Héritage Montréal's phrase, from golden age to urban decay in fifty years. Attrition, as English Wikipedia states it citing Rémillard and Merrett's Mansions of the Golden Square Mile (1987): "By 1983, only 30% of the mansions in the northern half of the Square Mile had survived demolition; and only 5% survived south of Sherbrooke Street." Héritage Montréal's own page carries a more cautious version — "Only about 30% of the bourgeois homes survived, north of Sherbrooke Street" — with neither the year nor the 5%. Whichever figure is right, the surviving stock is a remnant, and Héritage Montréal states that the ensemble "does not have a designation or specific strategy to protect and promote its heritage over current urban development considerations".

phase_title: The Mille carré doré and the Victorian terrace
name_fr: Maison en rangée de pierre grise
source_ref: RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005)

siting_landscape: Contiguous, in series, on the streets around the villas rather than on the villa streets themselves — the cahier is explicit that these were built for the middle class, on the streets neighbouring the Shaughnessy villas. | Very dense fabric in the Village Lincoln, where the cahier says it is the terraces and the individual heritage houses together that make the sector exceptional.
massing: Two and a half storeys.
articulation: Not stated for the Village Shaughnessy terraces beyond their Second Empire inspiration. | In the Milton Park half the Plateau cahier records decoration that is often elaborate, and Héritage Montréal describes great architectural diversity, with large single-family Victorian houses standing cheek by jowl with duplexes, triplexes and apartment houses.
openings: Not stated by any of the three sources.
materials: Stone, or sometimes brick, on the principal façade. | In Milton Park, grey stone or red sandstone.
blurb_en: The middle-class counterpart to the mansion, and the form this project has already recorded in Westmount: contiguous single-family houses in series, two and a half storeys, stone — sometimes brick — on the principal façade, mostly Second Empire in inspiration, built between 1870 and 1910 on the streets around the Shaughnessy villas and between 1875 and 1900 in Milton Park north of Sherbrooke. Many were later subdivided into two dwellings or more, which is why so much of this stock now reads as plex without ever having been built as one.
origin_en: Two halves of one form, on either side of a borough boundary that did not exist when it was built. South of Sherbrooke, the Village Shaughnessy: John Ostell's 1842 master plan turned development north-west, rues Chomedey and Lambert-Closse were cut about 1880, and between 1870 and 1910 the streets around the surviving villas filled with row houses for the middle class, with good maisons de rapport of the 1920s among them. North of Sherbrooke, Milton Park, which the Plateau cahier reads as the same building repeated — the contiguous one- or two-family house in grey stone or red sandstone, 1875–1900, later subdivided. The two halves went in opposite directions after 1945. Shaughnessy Village lost its villas one by one and was renamed a quartier; Milton Park was bought up by a single developer, threatened with total demolition, and bought back by its residents. See the notes at the foot of this page.

phase_title: Warehouses, maisons-magasins and the faubourgs
source_ref: RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005)
source_generation: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005), historical chapter printed pp. 29–30, and sector fiches 24.I.1, 24.I.5, 24.I.6, 24.I.9, 24.I.10, 24.I.11 and 24.I.12; with RPCQ fiche 93528, which lists the porte cochère among the characteristic elements of the declared site.
siting_landscape: Small lots on blocks laid out without a ruelle, which is the whole of the type's logic: with no service lane, access to the rear of the lot has to be taken through the building. | The carriage gate gives on to houses standing at the back of the yard and to fuel storage. | Deep lots, in 24.I.6 and 24.I.9, with rear-yard annexes since demolished; front yards where the ground floor stands clear of the ground. | The quarters that grew round the Molson brewery, the Canadian Rubber and the MacDonald Tobacco works.
massing: Two or three storeys. | Fine cornices, and in 24.I.5 false cornices.
articulation: Elaborate cornices, carriage gates and exterior stairs, in the cahier's own list for 24.I.6. | Elaborate crownings, slate roofs and dormers with worked joinery on the brick and grey-stone ensembles near rue Ontario (24.I.4).
openings: Vertical windows. | The carriage gate itself — a full-height arched opening in the street front, still visible throughout the sector. | Access to the ground floor fixes the front setback: none where the access is internal, set back where a stair on the façade has to be accommodated (24.I.4).
materials: Brick as the principal facing. | Grey stone or brick on the finer ensembles.
blurb_en: The eastern alternative to the ruelle, and the one detail in this borough that exists nowhere else on this site. Where the blocks around the Molson brewery, the Canadian Rubber and the MacDonald Tobacco works were cut into small lots with no service lane behind them, the only way to the back of the lot is through the building — so a full-height carriage gate is driven through the street front. Behind it are houses standing at the back of the yard and the coal and wood store. Two or three storeys, brick, vertical windows, elaborate cornices; the front setback is decided by nothing more than whether the stair to the upper dwellings is inside or out.
origin_en: The cahier gives the mechanism in the middle of its historical chapter, describing the dense population that gathered round the Molson brewery — in the quarter since the 18th century — the Canadian Rubber and the MacDonald Tobacco works: « Les quartiers qui entourent ces usines se composent de petits lots, et les quadrilatères (îlots) sont sans ruelle. Dans ce type de lotissement, c'est la porte cochère, toujours visible dans ce secteur, qui donne accès aux maisons en fond de cour ainsi qu'à l'entreposage de combustibles. » Set that against the Sud-Ouest, where Montréal's regulation of residential construction from about 1880 produced blocks with ruelles first in an « I » and then in an « H », and where the same regulation pushed the stair to the upper dwellings out of the building and into the front yard. Two solutions to one problem — how to reach the back of a deep, narrow lot — separated by a generation of by-laws and four kilometres of city. The carriage gate is the older answer, and Centre-Sud is where it survives; the RPCQ lists it among the characteristic elements of the declared site as well.

origin_en: This is the borough's link to the rural Québec forms catalogued elsewhere on this site — the small village house of Charlesbourg's Trait-Carré, of Île d'Orléans, of Lévis. Here it is a survivor inside a twentieth-century street grid rather than the parent of what came after: nothing in Villeray's plex or shoebox descends from it. The by-law's ordering makes the point by putting it first and then never referring back to it.

blurb_en: A single-storey brick box on a lot deeper than it is wide, set end-on and close to the street with the yard behind, its door in the middle and one tall window either side, and a cornice or a pedimented parapet raising the front above the flat roof. Built cheaply from what was to hand between 1900 and 1940, mostly in Villeray and Parc-Extension, and built to be built over later.
origin_en: The shoebox is the one self-built type on this site, and this is one of three records for it — with Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie's single type and with fiche 1.3 next door. The scholarly account is Guy Gaudreau, "Les premières maisons shoebox montréalaises de Rosemont et de Villeray" (Revue d'histoire urbaine / Urban History Review, DOI 10.3138/uhr-2020-0004), which pairs the same two boroughs this site now pairs. What is distinctive here is that the by-law does not simply describe the type: it regulates it, giving it three lettered variants and a table of permitted original and replacement components running to three further pages.

siting_landscape: Sited contiguously, detached or semi-detached. | Generally found on lots deeper than they are wide — the same lot geometry as the shoebox.

blurb_en: Two storeys of open-slat wood frame put up fast in a boom, under a flat roof or one falling gently to the back, with a stepped parapet on the side walls and a high pedimented or corniced parapet on the front that makes the building look taller than it is. A covered gallery runs the width of the façade. The by-law's own word for the effect is postiche — false-fronted.
origin_en: Boomtown is the most widely distributed form on this site, and this record is one of its two Montréal borough entries in Part 10. What this borough adds to the file is the frame: the fiche gives the construction method in plain French — a slatted wood frame, easy to build, quick to raise — where the Charlesbourg plan de conservation names it « une charpente claire, aussi appelée "Balloon Frame" » and most other sources describe only the parapet. The two readings belong together: the parapet is what the fast frame made possible to dress up.

articulation: The façade composition is symmetrical, and the dwelling doors — reached from the ground-floor or second-storey perron — are generally placed centrally. | The façade is punctuated by projections, above all balconies at every level. | The curved stair giving access to the upper balcony is named by the by-law as an important architectural characteristic of the type. | A marquise may cover the top-floor balcony. | Ornament is usual — brick bond patterns, worked lintels and sills. The crown varies from building to building but is generally a pedimented parapet under a moulded flashing.
openings: Windows aligned vertically and of vertical proportion.
materials: Brick, with stone; the ornament is worked in the brickwork itself as much as applied to it.
blurb_en: Montréal's own building, as this borough regulates it: two or three storeys of stacked flats under a flat roof, filling a narrow deep lot in a contiguous row with barely any setback, each dwelling with its own door on the front, balconies at every level, and a curved exterior stair climbing to the upper one. Ornament in the brickwork, worked lintels and sills, and a pedimented parapet on top. Villeray from about 1900, Parc-Extension from the 1920s.
origin_en: This is the plex family recorded in the words of the borough that has most of it. Two things here are not in the other Montréal plex records on this site. One is the borough's own social account of who lived in them — « logeaient les familles ouvrières qui travaillaient, notamment, dans les nombreuses carrières de pierre que l'on retrouvait à l'époque sur le territoire de l'arrondissement » — which ties the type to the Saint-Michel limestone quarries recorded as this borough's only archaeological interest. The other is that the by-law makes the curved exterior stair a named characteristic of a regulated type, which is what the shared explainer at /topics/escalier-exterieur/ exists to unpack.

source_generation: By-law Annexe F, fiche 3.1, pp. 3.1.1 to 3.1.5, transcribed verbatim, with the family definition from the 3.0 divider page

massing: Distinguished by its imposing gabarit, generally three storeys under a flat roof. | The ground floor is raised above the street and habitable rooms may be in the basement. | Projecting volumes on the façade are sometimes present.
articulation: The façade composition is generally symmetrical. | One central front door near ground level gives access to all the apartments — the single feature that separates this family from the plex. | Ornament is characteristic of these buildings, with the front door emphasised by a substantial stone architrave. | Façades may carry brick bond patterns, worked lintels and concrete bands. | The crown varies but often includes a pedimented parapet with acroteria under a moulded flashing.

blurb_en: The conciergerie: three storeys of flats between 1900 and 1940, imposing on its lot with only a shallow setback, more than a dozen dwellings reached from one central door at street level by a common interior stair. Ornament is the point — a heavy stone surround at that door, patterned brickwork, worked lintels, concrete bands, and a pedimented parapet with acroteria on top.
origin_en: The apartment building appears on this site under several names — maison d'appartements, conciergerie, édifice de rapport, walk-up — and this borough numbers all three of its generations. What this record adds is the definition by stair. Everywhere else on this site the apartment building is separated from the plex by counting dwellings; here it is separated by asking whether the stair is inside the plan, and the by-law says in as many words that putting it inside « rompt avec la tradition montréalaise des escaliers extérieurs ».
